modules.default_title: Lipid Management — CV Risk & Statin Prescribing
modules.landing_intro: Clinical decision support for lipid management and cardiovascular risk reduction in primary care. Use this module when evaluating a new patient on lipid therapy, initiating statins, or reviewing a patient not at LDL goal. Content is based on the AHA/ACC PREVENT Calculator (2023) and the 2018 AHA/ACC Cholesterol Guidelines.

context_strip.label: Organizational Standard
context_strip.text: AHA/ACC PREVENT Calculator is the required organizational risk stratification tool, replacing Pooled Cohort Equations. Epic BPA integration targeting October/November 2026. Until live, calculate manually at acc.org/PREVENT. SUPD (Statin Use in Persons with Diabetes) is a tracked VBC metric — HEDIS benchmark ~90%. All diabetic patients must have statin therapy addressed and documented at each visit.

faqs.title: Calculating ASCVD risk with the PREVENT Calculator

items.question: Why is PREVENT replacing the Pooled Cohort Equations?
items.answer_html: PREVENT incorporates kidney function (eGFR) and metabolic factors, and removes race as a variable — reducing known overestimation in certain populations. It is the 2023 AHA/ACC standard and Crystal Run's required organizational tool.

items.question: What are the four risk tiers and their thresholds?
items.answer_html: Low: <5% — no statin indicated. Borderline: 5–7.5% — shared decision-making; statin reasonable if LDL ≥70 plus risk enhancers. Intermediate: 7.5–20% — initiate statin. High: >20% — high-intensity statin, no shared decision-making required.

items.question: What are risk-enhancing factors for borderline-risk patients?
items.answer_html: Family history of premature ASCVD, hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L, ABI <0.9, elevated Lp(a) or ApoB. Presence of any of these at borderline risk (5–7.5%) with LDL ≥70 mg/dL supports statin initiation.

faqs.title: When and how to initiate statin therapy

items.question: When is high-intensity statin indicated without shared decision-making?
items.answer_html: Two automatic indications: (1) 10-year risk >20%, or (2) LDL ≥190 mg/dL regardless of risk score. Both are standard of care — document and initiate without requiring patient agreement process beyond standard informed consent.

items.question: When is shared decision-making required?
items.answer_html: All borderline-risk patients (5–7.5%). Document the conversation, the patient's preference, and the clinical factors considered. CAC score may support or defer initiation — CAC of 0 supports deferral; CAC >100 or ≥75th percentile supports initiation.

items.question: What is the SUPD requirement for diabetic patients?
items.answer_html: Statin Use in Persons with Diabetes is a HEDIS-tracked VBC metric with an organizational benchmark of ~90%. Every diabetic patient must have statin therapy addressed and documented at each visit, even if the patient declines or is intolerant.

faqs.title: LDL goals by risk tier

items.question: What are the LDL targets by tier?
items.answer_html: Very High Risk: <55 mg/dL. High Risk: <70 mg/dL. Intermediate Risk: <70–100 mg/dL depending on risk-enhancing factors. Borderline Risk: Shared decision-making — statin reasonable when LDL ≥70 plus risk enhancers.

items.question: What defines Very High Risk?
items.answer_html: Established ASCVD plus a second major cardiovascular event, OR one prior ASCVD event plus any of the following: diabetes, CKD, poorly controlled hypertension, current smoking, or LDL ≥100 mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin. Note: prior MI alone is High Risk; any comorbidity escalates to Very High Risk.

faqs.title: Documenting the medication plan and follow-up

items.question: What must be included in the medication plan documentation?
items.answer_html: Current statin name and intensity (low / moderate / high), whether patient is at LDL goal, next step if not at goal (intensify statin, add ezetimibe, or refer), and planned follow-up interval. Fasting lipid panel at 4–12 weeks after any change is standard.

items.question: What statin intensity classifications are used?
items.answer_html: High-intensity: Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg, Atorvastatin 40–80 mg. Moderate-intensity: Rosuvastatin 5–10 mg, Atorvastatin 10–20 mg, Simvastatin 20–40 mg. Low-intensity: Simvastatin 10 mg, Pravastatin 10–20 mg — generally insufficient for high or very high risk patients.

faqs.title: Managing severely elevated LDL

items.question: What action is required for LDL ≥190 mg/dL?
items.answer_html: Initiate high-intensity statin immediately — no shared decision-making required, no risk score threshold applies. Consider evaluation for familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). If LDL remains ≥100 mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin, add ezetimibe and consider PCSK9 inhibitor referral to cardiology.

faqs.title: Escalation pathway when LDL goal is not met

items.question: What is the escalation sequence when a patient is not at LDL goal?
items.answer_html: Step 1: Confirm adherence and maximize statin dose. Step 2: Add ezetimibe 10 mg daily — proven LDL reduction of 15–20%. Step 3: If still not at goal, refer to cardiology for PCSK9 inhibitor consideration (alirocumab, evolocumab). PCSK9 inhibitors require prior authorization and documented statin intolerance or failure.

faqs.title: Using CAC scoring to guide shared decision-making

items.question: When is CAC scoring appropriate?
items.answer_html: Ages 40–75 with borderline to intermediate risk (5–20%) who are hesitant about statin initiation. CAC of 0 supports deferral with reassessment in 5–7 years. CAC >100 or ≥75th percentile for age/sex supports initiation. Document the CAC result and the patient's decision in the chart.

items.question: Is CAC covered by insurance?
items.answer_html: Coverage confirmation is pending with the payer team. Verify before ordering. Cost is typically $75–150 out of pocket when not covered.

faqs.title: When to escalate from High to Very High Risk

items.question: What triggers Very High Risk reclassification?
items.answer_html: Established ASCVD plus a second major event, OR any prior ASCVD event combined with: diabetes, CKD, poorly controlled hypertension, current smoking, or LDL ≥100 mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin. Reclassification changes LDL target from <70 to <55 mg/dL and makes PCSK9 inhibitor referral appropriate if goal is not met.

items.question: Is cardiology referral required for Very High Risk patients?
items.answer_html: Not automatically required, but strongly consider referral when LDL goal (<55 mg/dL) is not being met on maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe.

faqs.title: ApoB and Lp(a) — when and how to order

items.question: When are ApoB and Lp(a) indicated?
items.answer_html: ApoB: Indicated for High and Very High Risk patients to assess residual risk beyond LDL, particularly when LDL appears controlled but cardiovascular risk remains unclear. Lp(a): Indicated once per lifetime for all patients with premature ASCVD, strong family history, or LDL ≥190 not fully explained by diet/secondary causes.

items.question: Is ordering ApoB or Lp(a) currently approved?
items.answer_html: Coverage and indications are pending confirmation with the payer team. Do not embed in order sets or SmartSets until confirmed. Manual ordering with documented clinical indication is acceptable in the interim.

modules.landing_intro: A patient has an abnormal creatinine, or you've ordered cystatin C and the eGFR came back lower than expected. Use this checklist to complete a reasonable initial workup before escalating. Nephrology should receive a patient you've already started working — not one you're handing off cold.
modules.checklist_section_label: Before you escalate — complete all four

checklist.statement: Review current medication list for nephrotoxins and renally-cleared drugs requiring dose adjustment
Establish baseline: order cystatin C if not yet done, BMP, CBC, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR), urinalysis with microscopy
Stage the CKD using cystatin C-based eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021) and albuminuria category — document G and A stage
Blood pressure at goal for CKD (< 120/80 if tolerated) — document current readings and agent

green_zone.zone_label: All boxes checked — You've done the work
green_zone.narrative_html: Initial workup complete. Document staging and baseline using SmartPhrase below. Safe to manage stage G1–G3a with standard interventions while awaiting nephrology input if needed. You are institutionally supported.

modules.escalation_section_label: Escalate to nephrology e-consult if any apply

escalation.statement: eGFR decline > 5 mL/min/1.73m² in 12 months, or > 10 in 24 months
eGFR < 30 (G4–G5) at any point
uACR > 300 mg/g (severely increased albuminuria)
Unexplained CKD — no clear etiology after initial workup (no diabetes, no hypertension, no obstructive history)
Persistent hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs on microscopy

faqs.title: Nephrotoxins and dose-adjusted drugs — what to look for

items.question: What medications should I flag immediately?
items.answer_html:
High-priority nephrotoxins to review in any CKD patient:

NSAIDs (including OTC ibuprofen/naproxen) — counsel to discontinue.

Metformin — generally safe to eGFR 30, reduce monitoring frequency below 45, hold below 30.

SGLT2 inhibitors — reassess below eGFR 45 (varies by agent and indication).

ACE inhibitors / ARBs — do not discontinue for mild creatinine bump (up to 30% rise is acceptable and expected); do reassess if rise exceeds that threshold.

Gabapentin/pregabalin — dose reduction required below eGFR 60.

Renally-cleared antibiotics — flag for any acute prescribing: nitrofurantoin contraindicated below eGFR 45.

items.question: My patient is on an NSAID for chronic pain. Do I stop it today?
items.answer_html:
In CKD G3a and above (eGFR < 60), the recommendation is to discontinue chronic NSAID use. Have a direct conversation: frame it as protecting kidney function, not removing pain management.

Offer alternatives — acetaminophen, topical diclofenac for localized pain, or a warm handoff to pain management if the underlying condition warrants it. Document the conversation and the plan.

items.question: Should I adjust doses myself or wait for nephrology?
items.answer_html:
For common medications with well-established renal dosing (metformin, gabapentin, many antibiotics), adjust now using the eGFR-based thresholds above. Do not wait for nephrology to make changes that are your responsibility as the PCP.

The e-consult is for guidance on management strategy — not for permission to stop nephrotoxins.

faqs.title: What to order and why — the CKD baseline panel

items.question: Why cystatin C if I already have a creatinine-based eGFR?
items.answer_html:
Creatinine-based eGFR is affected by muscle mass, diet, and race — it systematically overestimates GFR in patients with low muscle mass (elderly, frail, malnourished) and can underestimate in bodybuilders.

Cystatin C is filtered at a constant rate regardless of these variables. The CKD-EPI 2021 equation using both markers is now the preferred standard. When cystatin C eGFR is meaningfully lower than creatinine eGFR, believe cystatin C — it's the more accurate number.

items.question: My patient's cystatin C eGFR came back 15 points lower than their creatinine eGFR. Is that real?
items.answer_html:
Often yes. This is the most common anxiety point with cystatin C adoption. The lower number is not an error — it's a more accurate reflection of true GFR, particularly in older or leaner patients.

Stage and manage based on the cystatin C result. If this moves the patient into a higher-risk category, that's exactly the information you needed.

items.question: What does the uACR add?
items.answer_html:
Albuminuria is an independent risk factor for CKD progression and cardiovascular disease, separate from eGFR. A patient can have eGFR 65 with uACR > 300 and be at higher risk than a patient with eGFR 52 and uACR < 30.

Staging requires both dimensions — the G stage (eGFR) and the A stage (albuminuria). You cannot complete a CKD staging without it.

items.question: Does the urinalysis with microscopy need to be a fresh catch?
items.answer_html:
Ideally yes — a fresh midstream catch within 2 hours of collection gives the most reliable microscopy, particularly for RBC morphology. If the patient is in office, collect it that day.

If ordering remotely, instruct accordingly and note in the order.

faqs.title: Staging with cystatin C eGFR — what the numbers mean

items.question: What are the GFR stages and what do they mean clinically?
items.answer_html:
Using CKD-EPI 2021 cystatin C-based eGFR:

G1: ≥ 90 — Normal or high. CKD diagnosis requires other markers (albuminuria, structural abnormality). Monitor.

G2: 60–89 — Mildly decreased. Monitor annually if stable.

G3a: 45–59 — Mildly to moderately decreased. Begin medication review, BP optimization, RAAS therapy if proteinuric.

G3b: 30–44 — Moderately to severely decreased. Nephrology e-consult appropriate. Begin anemia workup, mineral/bone disease labs.

G4: 15–29 — Severely decreased. Nephrology referral (not just e-consult). RRT planning discussion begins.

G5: < 15 — Kidney failure. Active nephrology co-management required.

items.question: My patient is G3a. What do I actually do at this visit?
items.answer_html:
Three things: (1) Start or optimize an ACE inhibitor or ARB if they have albuminuria or diabetes — this is the single highest-impact intervention in early CKD. (2) Get BP below 120/80 if tolerated. (3) Counsel on nephrotoxin avoidance and dietary sodium restriction.

An SGLT2 inhibitor is indicated if they have diabetes or heart failure — this is now a standard of care intervention, not a specialist decision.

items.question: Do I need to tell the patient they have CKD?
items.answer_html:
Yes — this is a diagnosis, and it should be documented and communicated as such. Many patients with CKD G3 have been managed for years without anyone saying the words. Naming it clearly allows the patient to understand the stakes, engage in self-management, and make informed decisions.

Use plain language: "Your kidneys are working at about X% of normal. This is a condition called chronic kidney disease. It's manageable and we caught it at a stage where we can do a lot to protect them."

faqs.title: BP targets in CKD — tighter than you might think

items.question: Is 130/80 good enough?
items.answer_html:
Current KDIGO 2021 guidelines recommend a target of < 120 mmHg systolic if tolerated, based on SPRINT trial data. This is a meaningful shift from the older 130/80 standard.

In practice, tolerability is the limiting factor — orthostatic symptoms, syncope risk in elderly patients, and baseline hypotension all require individualization. Document your target and your rationale.

items.question: Which agents are preferred?
items.answer_html:
ACE inhibitor or ARB is first-line in CKD with albuminuria (uACR > 30) or diabetes, regardless of BP. Do not use both together — dual RAAS blockade increases harm without added benefit.

For additional BP control: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) and thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone preferred over HCTZ in CKD) are appropriate add-ons. Loop diuretics for volume management in G4–G5.

items.question: My patient's creatinine bumped after I started the ACE inhibitor. Should I stop it?
items.answer_html:
Not automatically. A rise in creatinine of up to 30% after initiating an ACE inhibitor or ARB is expected, acceptable, and does not indicate harm — it reflects the intended hemodynamic effect on the glomerulus.

Recheck in 2 weeks. If the rise is greater than 30% or potassium rises above 5.5, then hold and reassess. If you stop every ACE inhibitor that causes any creatinine bump, you will deprive CKD patients of their most protective therapy.

faqs.title: eGFR declining faster than expected — what to do

items.question: How do I know if the decline is rapid?
items.answer_html:
Pull prior creatinine values from the chart — at minimum 12 months back, ideally 24. Calculate the trajectory. A decline of more than 5 mL/min/1.73m² per year is considered rapid and warrants e-consult regardless of current stage.

A single low value without prior data is not the same as demonstrated progression — establish the trend first.

items.question: Could something acute be driving this?
items.answer_html:
Yes — always rule out AKI superimposed on CKD before concluding progression. Recent illness, volume depletion, new nephrotoxin exposure, or urinary obstruction can all cause acute drops.

If there's any question, recheck in 4–6 weeks after addressing potential acute factors before framing as progression.

faqs.title: eGFR < 30 — escalation and preparation

items.question: What changes at G4?
items.answer_html:
Several things happen simultaneously at G4 that go beyond standard PCP management:

(1) Nephrology referral (not just e-consult) is indicated. (2) Mineral and bone disease workup: PTH, phosphorus, 25-OH vitamin D, calcium. (3) Anemia of CKD evaluation. (4) RRT planning conversation — not to alarm, but to inform. Patients who arrive at dialysis having never discussed it are poorly prepared.

items.question: Should I be starting erythropoiesis-stimulating agents?
items.answer_html:
ESA initiation in CKD is a nephrology decision. Your role at G4 is to identify anemia, complete the workup (iron studies, B12, folate, retic count), correct iron deficiency if present, and document.

The e-consult to nephrology should include this workup so they can advise on ESA candidacy with full information in hand.

faqs.title: Severely increased albuminuria — uACR > 300

items.question: Is this nephrotic range?
items.answer_html:
Not necessarily — nephrotic range proteinuria is traditionally defined as > 3.5 g/day on 24-hour urine, or roughly uACR > 2000–3500 mg/g. A uACR of 300–2000 is severely increased but not nephrotic.

However, any uACR > 300 warrants e-consult regardless of eGFR, as it indicates significant glomerular pathology and accelerated progression risk.

items.question: Should I repeat it before acting?
items.answer_html:
A single elevated uACR should be confirmed on a second sample (ideally first morning void) before staging — transient elevations occur with fever, exercise, and UTI.

However, if the value is markedly elevated (> 300) and there's no obvious transient cause, begin the workup in parallel with confirmation rather than waiting.

faqs.title: CKD without a clear cause

items.question: My patient has CKD but no diabetes, no hypertension, no obstructive history. What now?
items.answer_html:
This is the e-consult indication — unexplained CKD requires nephrology input to consider glomerulonephritis, genetic nephropathy, or other primary renal disease.

Before the consult, complete: urinalysis with microscopy (looking for casts), uACR, renal ultrasound, serum protein electrophoresis in patients > 40 (to screen for myeloma), ANA and complement if clinical picture suggests autoimmune.

Document what you've ruled out — the nephrologist can then focus on what remains.

faqs.title: Persistent hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs

items.question: What do dysmorphic RBCs mean?
items.answer_html:
Dysmorphic RBCs — particularly acanthocytes — on urine microscopy indicate glomerular origin of bleeding, as opposed to urothelial sources (stone, tumor, infection). This is a nephrology finding, not a urology finding.

If the microscopy report specifically mentions dysmorphic RBCs or acanthocytes, the e-consult goes to nephrology, not to urology for cystoscopy.

items.question: What if the report just says "RBCs present" without commenting on morphology?
items.answer_html:
Standard urinalysis does not assess morphology — that requires microscopy with a trained eye. If you have > 5 RBCs/hpf on two separate specimens without an obvious benign cause, request formal microscopy.

In many practices this requires a specific order or a call to the lab.

modules.landing_intro: A new or transitioning patient is on stimulant medication. Use this checklist to determine whether to continue, document, or escalate. Tap any item for guidance.
modules.checklist_section_label: Before you decide — verify all four

checklist.statement: PDMP reviewed — no concerning pattern
No active substance use disorder (or documented awareness & plan)
Medication appears effective — patient functional, no recent dose escalation requests
No early fill requests in the past 12 months

green_zone.narrative_html: Continue current regimen. Document using SmartPhrase below. You are institutionally supported.

modules.escalation_section_label: Escalate to psychiatry e-consult if any apply

escalation.statement: Diagnosis based on self-report alone — no prior formal workup documented
Dose at or near ceiling, or recently escalated without documented clinical rationale
Functional decline or behavioral red flags despite medication
Patient requesting combination stimulants or multi-agent regimen

context_strip.label: National context
context_strip.text: Primary care providers across the US manage a meaningful proportion of adult ADHD stimulant prescriptions. You are not an outlier for inheriting these patients. The question is not whether to manage — it is how to manage safely. No US guideline (AAP, AAFP, AACAP, APA) addresses the inherited adult-stimulant scenario directly; this module adapts the CDC 2022 opioid inherited-prescription stewardship approach (Recommendation 5) to ADHD stimulants because no ADHD-specific US framework exists.[ref:cdc-opioid-2022][ref:aafp-2024][ref:aap-wolraich2019] The NICE NG87 shared-care model is UK-only and has no direct US analog.[ref:nice-ng87][ref:bjgp-price2024]

modules.footer_note: This is a viable first pathway, not the only pathway. Experienced providers retain clinical discretion. This framework provides institutional backing when followed. Regulatory prose covers New York and New Jersey explicitly (PDMP rules differ between the two states); providers in other jurisdictions should verify their state's controlled-substance requirements with their compliance office. Numeric early-fill thresholds referenced in this module reflect PBM/pharmacy dispensing convention rather than clinical or regulatory guideline; they are flagged as such where they appear. Verify current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

faqs.title: What counts as a "concerning pattern"?

items.question: How often should I check the PDMP?
items.answer_html:
The answer is state-conditional. ADHD stimulants are Schedule II under federal CSA scheduling.[ref:usc-21-812]

New York Under NY Public Health Law §3343-a (I-STOP), every practitioner must consult the PMP registry prior to prescribing or dispensing any Schedule II, III, or IV controlled substance. Schedule V is not covered by the duty. For an inherited adult-stimulant patient on routine 30-day fills, this means a PMP check before every prescribing event, not quarterly.[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:istop-blum2016][ref:istop-virani2018] Statutory exceptions to the duty include veterinarians, on-premises institutional dispensing, ED prescribing of ≤5-day supply, hospice patients, and certain technical-failure or waiver situations.[ref:ny-pbh-3343a]

New Jersey Under NJSA 45:1-46.1 (P.L.2017 c.341), NJ PMP access is required at three trigger points: (a) the first-time prescription of a Schedule II controlled substance or any opioid for acute or chronic pain to a new patient; (b) the first-time prescription of a Schedule III/IV benzodiazepine to a new patient; and (c) quarterly during the period the patient continues to receive such prescriptions.[ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1] NJ's per-prescription consultation duty is narrower than New York's — initial plus quarterly is the operational standard for ongoing Schedule II ADHD therapy in NJ.

The older module language framing "quarterly checks at prescription renewal visits" as a reasonable standard for stable patients is incorrect for New York and is a partial fit for New Jersey. Use the per-prescription standard in NY and the initial-plus-quarterly standard in NJ; both are minimums, and best practice is at least a check at every renewal visit regardless of state.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:cdc-opioid-2022]

Verify current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

items.question: What specifically am I looking for?
items.answer_html:
The patterns below are observational signals worth investigating, not algorithmic verdicts. PDMPs display dispensed data, not prescriber intent — partial fills, payor changes, and the 2022–2024 stimulant shortage all create patterns that look concerning at first glance and resolve into nothing on closer inspection.[ref:asam-pdmp-2023][ref:delcher-fadingsignal-2021] Treat the PDMP as a starting point for clarification with the patient, not a verdict.

Patterns that warrant a closer look:

Overlapping prescribers — multiple prescribers within an overlapping time window without documented coordination is the load-bearing concern, not multi-prescriber patterns per se. Care transitions, specialist consultations, and PCP changes routinely produce sequential multi-prescriber records that are entirely benign.[ref:cdc-opioid-2022][ref:delcher-doctorshopping-2022]

Multiple pharmacies without clear reason — research thresholds for "shopping" patterns generally use ≥4 pharmacies (often ≥4 prescribers AND ≥4 pharmacies in the same window).[ref:young-painmed-2018][ref:chua-jamaopen-2019][ref:delcher-doctorshopping-2022] An ADHD-specific analysis of stimulant doctor-shopping (Cepeda 2015) found a prevalence of just 0.4% with a distinct signature: median travel of 91.9 miles vs. 0.2 miles for non-shoppers, 28% multi-state, and 27% paid cash.[ref:cepeda-ajdaa-2015] Routine multi-pharmacy fills driven by insurance, geography, or a stockout substitution are not the signal.

Concurrent opioid prescription — warrants clarification rather than reflexive concern. Roughly 14% of stimulant-treated ADHD patients receive an opioid prescription within a year; SUD history elevates that further (aHR 1.69).[ref:shrestha-annpharm-2026][ref:wei-jamaopen-2018] Concurrent opioid + stimulant use without a documented pain rationale or specialist coordination has been associated with elevated overdose risk in some cohorts (HR 2.02 in one),[ref:palis-bmcph-2022][ref:lee-lancetam-2025] but the picture is not uniform — outpatient stimulant-positive UDS in patients on long-term opioids was not significantly associated with opioid-related ED visits in another cohort,[ref:appa-dad-2024] and a Canadian cohort on opioid agonist therapy found buprenorphine + prescribed stimulants associated with reduced overdose risk (aHR 0.47) — directly contradicting the assumption that any stimulant + OUD-treatment combination is high-risk.[ref:young-bc-addiction-2025] Confirm the indication; do not reflexively discontinue.

Dose-quantity discrepancy — total quantities dispensed across all sources that exceed what would be expected for a single therapeutic regimen warrant clarification through patient discussion and prescriber coordination. Note that dispensed data conflates partial fills, returned medication, and stockout substitutions, especially during the 2022–2024 stimulant shortage; "mismatch" is not the same as diversion.[ref:cdc-opioid-2022]

False-positive caveat — a 2021 analysis of opioid "shopper" patterns found roughly 20% of flagged patients had a cancer diagnosis by 2017 (a "fading signal" pattern). Look for the true signature; do not reflexively flag.[ref:delcher-fadingsignal-2021]

Reassuring pattern — same prescriber, same pharmacy, consistent quantity, no gaps suggesting diversion, no overlapping controlled-substance prescriptions from other providers in the same therapeutic class.

items.question: I see something concerning. What do I do?
items.answer_html:
Do not prescribe at this visit. Have a direct, non-accusatory conversation with the patient: "I'm seeing some things in the prescription history I want to understand before we go further."

Document exactly what you found and what the patient told you. This is protective for you and the institution regardless of what you decide next.

If the concern is significant, this is an appropriate trigger for an e-consult to psychiatry with the specific question of safe prescribing plan rather than routine review.

items.question: The prior provider didn't document any PDMP checks. Does that mean I'm starting over?
items.answer_html:
Yes — when you become the prescriber of record, the documentation obligation transfers to you. The prior provider's omission is their liability, not yours, but it does mean your first check is essential before issuing your first prescription.

Think of it as a brief triage at the first handoff appointment. It takes under two minutes and is your best protection.

faqs.title: What if there's a substance use disorder in the history?

items.question: The patient has a past SUD. Is that a dealbreaker?
items.answer_html:
Not automatically — and the evidence has shifted further than the older framing suggests. A past or even active substance-use disorder is a risk factor that warrants enhanced monitoring, not an automatic disqualifier. ASAM/AAAP (2024) explicitly support stimulant therapy in patients with co-occurring ADHD and substance-use disorder when benefits outweigh risks, with monitoring commensurate with risk.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:aaap-batki2023] A large retrospective analysis (Baweja 2025) of adolescents and young adults with co-occurring ADHD and SUD found stimulant treatment associated with fewer hospitalizations, lower suicidal-ideation/attempt rates (RR 0.63–0.79), and a 30% reduction in mortality (aHR 0.70) versus non-stimulant management; the same analysis flagged a clinician under-prescribing pattern (RR 0.63 of receiving stimulants in this population).[ref:baweja-jaacap-2025][ref:zelabowski-jcm-2025][ref:chamakalayil-fpsych-2020]

Tension worth knowing The AAFP 2024 review lists "drug addiction, alcohol misuse" among contraindications to stimulants, while ASAM/AAAP 2024 treats SUD as a risk factor requiring enhanced monitoring rather than a contraindication.[ref:aafp-2024][ref:asam-aaap-2024] The two are in real tension. Document which framework you're working from and why; ASAM/AAAP language is more clinically actionable in light of current outcome data, but AAFP language may dominate medicolegal expectations.

Specialist collaboration ASAM/AAAP recommend that stimulant prescribing in the context of co-occurring SUD ideally involve specialist-level addiction-medicine expertise or close specialist collaboration — not primary care acting alone.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:aaap-batki2023] Treat the e-consult here as clinical guidance, not just documentation: the question is monitoring intensity, formulation choice, and risk-stratification, not just whether to continue.

Note also: in patients on opioid agonist therapy, prescribed stimulants combined with buprenorphine were associated with reduced overdose risk (aHR 0.47) in a recent Canadian cohort — relevant to inherited patients carrying both an OUD treatment regimen and an ADHD stimulant prescription.[ref:young-bc-addiction-2025]

items.question: What does "documented awareness and plan" look like?
items.answer_html:
Reframe from "minimum documentation requirements" to "recommended monitoring elements." The PDMP cadence is state-driven (see the PDMP FAQ), and ASAM/AAAP rate the certainty of evidence for individual stimulant-misuse-prevention strategies as very low — these are reasonable practices that share an evidence base, not a fixed checklist.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:aaap-batki2023]

Recommended monitoring elements when SUD is in the picture:

ER or prodrug formulation preference When prescribing stimulants to patients with SUD history, ASAM/AAAP recommend preferentially using extended-release or prodrug formulations to reduce misuse and abuse potential.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:aaap-batki2023] This is the single most actionable formulation-level adjustment for an inherited patient already on an IR product.

PDMP review at the cadence required by your state (per-prescription in NY; initial + quarterly in NJ).[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1]

Urine drug screening as one tool among several, not as a mandatory or punitive practice. Discuss expectations with the patient up front.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:cdc-opioid-2022]

Pill counts and visit frequency Pill counts at random intervals and increased visit frequency are explicitly listed in ASAM/AAAP monitoring recommendations alongside PDMP and UDS.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:aaap-batki2023]

Documentation A note that the provider is aware of the SUD history, has considered it in the prescribing decision, and is using the monitoring elements above. Example language: "Patient has history of [SUD], currently in [active treatment / remission x timeframe]. Stimulant therapy reviewed in this context. Continued [ER/prodrug formulation] with close monitoring including PDMP review at each renewal, urine drug screen [frequency], and pill counts at [interval]." SmartPhrase .CSADHD-SUD-AWARE covers this documentation.

items.question: The patient currently uses cannabis. Does that count?
items.answer_html:
The clinically relevant distinction is between cannabis use and cannabis use disorder (CUD, DSM-5-TR). Mere use is common and generally non-actionable; CUD is clinically actionable.[ref:dsm-5-tr-2022][ref:ryan-jad-2025]

Prevalence anchors: in a community-based adult ADHD sample, ~75% had ever used cannabis and ~41% used in the past 30 days; among daily users, ~62% met criteria for CUD.[ref:ryan-jad-2025] Importantly, prescription stimulant misuse rates were comparable across daily and non-daily cannabis users (29% vs. 37%, ns) in that sample — daily cannabis use is not a reliable signal for stimulant-misuse risk on its own.[ref:ryan-jad-2025]

CUD changes the picture clinically Adult ADHD patients with cannabis use disorder show a substantially reduced response to ADHD pharmacotherapy (OR 0.20–0.24 versus those without CUD).[ref:carbone-jcm-2026] When CUD is present, expect attenuated treatment effect, address the CUD as a co-occurring disorder, and apply the SUD-aware monitoring framework above. Cannabis is not itself recommended as ADHD treatment.[ref:francisco-jpr-2023]

Practical framing: occasional or recreational cannabis use in a stable, well-functioning patient is a documentation point, not necessarily an escalation trigger. CUD is a co-occurring SUD and gets the SUD framework. Document your reasoning either way.

faqs.title: How do I assess whether the medication is actually working?

items.question: I'm inheriting the patient — I never saw them before treatment. How can I judge efficacy?
items.answer_html:
Honest framing first No US ADHD guideline (AAP, AAFP, AACAP, APA, state medical boards) addresses the inherited adult-stimulant scenario directly. The closest US analog is CDC 2022 opioid guideline Recommendation 5, which directs clinicians evaluating patients on inherited long-term opioid therapy to assess benefit-versus-risk of continuation rather than penalize the patient for accepting the current prescription.[ref:cdc-opioid-2022][ref:aafp-2024][ref:samhsa-tip63-2021] The NICE NG87 shared-care model is UK-only with no direct US analog.[ref:nice-ng87][ref:bjgp-price2024][ref:bmc-asherson2022] This module adapts that opioid-stewardship logic to ADHD stimulants because no ADHD-specific US framework exists. Naming that explicitly — to yourself and to the patient — is honest.

Practically, the assessment is a middle ground rather than a binary:

Review available records Even thin records often show prior childhood symptoms, prior ADHD evaluation, or a school-history note. A plausible diagnostic history (childhood-onset symptoms, prior structured evaluation of any kind) materially changes the picture.

Assess current function and treatment response Ask directly: "How are things going at work / school / home? What did the medication change for you, and what would change if you stopped?" Specific, credible improvements in function are a reasonable basis for continuation.[ref:aafp-2024]

Screen for misuse PDMP review, brief substance-use screening, and a check on red-flag patterns (early fills, multiple prescribers, etc.) at the inheritance visit. The full PDMP and SUD FAQs cover the specifics.

You are not re-validating the original diagnosis from scratch. You are verifying that the inherited prescription is delivering documented function and that the prescribing context is safe — exactly what CDC's inherited-opioid framework asks of a primary-care provider.[ref:cdc-opioid-2022]

items.question: The patient says it's working but I'm not sure I believe them.
items.answer_html:
This is a clinical judgment call that doesn't have a bright-line answer. A few considerations:

Is there corroboration? Prior notes from a previous provider, a therapist, a partner or employer? Even a prior rating scale in the chart?

Are there behavioral inconsistencies? Does the patient's presentation, history, or PDMP pattern suggest misuse or diversion rather than treatment?

If your clinical instinct is firing and you can't articulate why you're comfortable, that's the moment to pause, document, and consider an e-consult. That consult is not punitive — it's you doing exactly what the framework asks.

items.question: Should I be using a rating scale at follow-up visits?
items.answer_html:
Formal diagnostic rating scales — the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS), the Conners Adult ADHD Rating Scale — were designed for screening and initial evaluation, not routine treatment monitoring.[ref:asrs-ustun2017][ref:asrs-anbarasan2020] No US guideline mandates a formal rating scale at every follow-up; framing the absence of a scale as a deviation would overstate the evidence. This is consistent with clinical convention rather than an explicit guideline directive.[ref:aafp-2024][ref:ramsay-ndt-2017]

That said, the trend in ADHD care is toward measurement-based monitoring. Brief structured symptom and function assessment at each renewal — even a short checklist or a consistent set of functional questions — is recommended; AAFP suggests reevaluation at least every 3 months including symptom and function review.[ref:aafp-2024] Periodic use of a rating scale during titration or at a treatment change is supported and helpful.[ref:ramsay-ndt-2017]

The goal is reproducible documentation of treatment response over time, not a diagnostic workup at every visit. Pick a brief set of functional domains and side-effect questions and use them consistently.

faqs.title: Early fill requests — what's the threshold?

items.question: How early is "too early"?
items.answer_html:
Provenance note The "5-day early" threshold and the "2+ early fills in 12 months" pattern that circulate in primary care are PBM and pharmacy dispensing conventions — typically derived from a 75–80% days-supply edit on a 30-day prescription — not clinical guideline thresholds. CDC, SAMHSA, ASAM/AAAP, AAFP, FDA, and DEA do not specify a numeric early-fill cutoff for stimulants; ASAM/AAAP rates the certainty of evidence for all stimulant-misuse-prevention strategies as very low.[ref:asam-aaap-2024][ref:aaap-batki2023][ref:aafp-2024][ref:cdc-opioid-2022][ref:asam-prr-2021] Treat the numbers as institutional policy markers, not as evidence-based triggers.

Practically: a single early fill is worth documenting and may warrant a brief, nonjudgmental conversation. A pattern of repeated early fills warrants individualized clinical-risk assessment — not a fixed numeric trigger.

Context matters. A patient who filled early once because of a vacation schedule, a 2022–2024 stimulant-shortage substitution, or a partial fill that confounds the days-supply calculation is different from a patient with a consistent pattern across multiple cycles.[ref:asam-prr-2021]

Repeated early-fill pattern — document the pattern, address it directly with the patient, consider a urine drug screen, and review the PDMP. Whether the pattern crosses into "escalation" is a clinical judgment, not an algorithmic trigger.

items.question: Can I fill early for travel or vacation?
items.answer_html:
The framing that "Schedule II cannot be post-dated" is not correct at the federal level. Federal law (21 CFR §1306.12) prohibits refills of Schedule II prescriptions, but explicitly permits a practitioner to issue multiple sequential prescriptions totaling up to 90 days of supply, provided the practitioner indicates on each prescription (other than any first prescription intended to be filled immediately) the earliest date on which a pharmacy may fill that prescription.[ref:cfr-1306-12][ref:nysmidwife-osborne2017]

Each prescription must be issued for a legitimate medical purpose by an individual practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice (21 CFR §1306.04), and the practitioner must conclude that the practice does not create undue risk of diversion or abuse.[ref:cfr-1306-04] The prescriber writes the date and the "do not fill before" instruction; the pharmacy honors it.

The "early-fill window" the patient is bumping into is usually a PBM or pharmacy days-supply edit, not a state or federal statute.[ref:asam-prr-2021] State law may impose additional restrictions on top of the federal framework — verify state-level rules with your compliance office before issuing sequential post-dated Schedule II prescriptions.

For international travel, plan well ahead with the prescribing provider — destination-country import rules vary widely and may be more restrictive than US dispensing rules. Verify current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

items.question: The patient says they lost the medication. What do I do?
items.answer_html:
Federal law (21 CFR §1306.04, §1306.11–12; 21 USC §829) does not categorically prohibit a practitioner from issuing a new prescription when a patient reports a lost or stolen Schedule II medication. The validity of any new prescription is governed by §1306.04 — it must be issued for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice.[ref:cfr-1306-04][ref:cfr-1306-11][ref:cfr-1306-12][ref:usc-21-829]

Most institutions and practices nonetheless adopt a no-replacement policy for lost or stolen Schedule II medications as a risk-management standard.[ref:asam-risk2024] That is institutional policy, not federal regulation; communicate it honestly. Suggested phrasing: "Our practice doesn't replace lost or stolen Schedule II prescriptions as a matter of policy. The DEA framework allows me clinical discretion, but our institutional standard is no replacement, and that's how I have to handle this."

Document the report, check the PDMP, and note the conversation in the chart. A single loss event is not necessarily disqualifying for continued prescribing, but it belongs in the record. Repeated lost-prescription reports — especially clustered with other risk markers — change the clinical picture and warrant escalation.

Verify your institution's policy and current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

faqs.title: The prior diagnosis looks thin. Now what?

items.question: The chart has an ADHD diagnosis but no workup. Am I on the hook for that?
items.answer_html:
You are not responsible for the prior diagnostic process, but you are responsible for decisions made from this point forward. Continuing a prescription is a clinical decision — meaning it's yours, and it should be defensible.

The question isn't "was this diagnosis legitimate?" It's "do I have enough information to comfortably continue this medication?" If the answer is no, the e-consult pathway exists precisely for this situation.

items.question: What does a "formal workup" actually mean? Is neuropsychological testing required?
items.answer_html:
Neuropsychological testing is not required for ADHD diagnosis in most cases — ADHD is a clinical diagnosis based on history, symptoms, and functional impairment, and cognitive batteries alone have inadequate sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis.[ref:posner-lancet-2020][ref:nikolas-psychassess-2019] AAFP nonetheless lists neuropsychological testing as something that should be considered when (a) collateral information is lacking, (b) malingering is suspected, or (c) confounding psychiatric comorbidity is present.[ref:aafp-2024] Combined with a validated rating scale, cognitive testing improves specificity even though it is not a stand-alone diagnostic tool.[ref:marshall-clinneuropsych-2021][ref:nikolas-psychassess-2019]

A reasonable adult workup should include all of:

Validated rating scale ASRS or comparable, completed by the patient.[ref:asrs-ustun2017][ref:asrs-anbarasan2020]

Structured clinical interview Symptom onset (DSM-5-TR requires several inattentive/hyperactive-impulsive symptoms before age 12), duration, cross-setting impairment.[ref:dsm-5-tr-2022][ref:aafp-2024]

Collateral information Strongly recommended, not optional. Childhood medical or school records, school transcripts, prior work evaluations, and observer reports (parent, partner, employer) all carry diagnostic weight; self-report alone has poor specificity for adult ADHD diagnosis, and roughly 20% of prescription-stimulant misusers exaggerate symptoms in self-report.[ref:aafp-2024][ref:nejm-volkow2013][ref:marshall-clinneuropsych-2021] Even one or two of these data points materially change the picture.

Differential AND comorbidity Reframe the differential from "rule out alternatives" to "rule out AND identify co-occurring conditions." Anxiety, mood disorders, substance use disorders, sleep disorders, and thyroid disease can all mimic ADHD. They also commonly co-occur: in adult ADHD cohorts, the odds of comorbid anxiety, mood, and substance use disorders run 4.5–8.7 (Hartman 2023).[ref:hartman-nbr-2023] An adult ADHD diagnosis without a SUD screen is incomplete.

If none of this is in the chart, that's thin — but it's a very common chart. The e-consult purpose here is to get a psychiatrist's eyes on the case so you have expert documentation in the record. It changes the risk profile for both of you.

items.question: The patient is stable, functional, and has been on the medication for 5 years. Does the shaky diagnosis still matter?
items.answer_html:
A long stable course with demonstrated functional benefit is one important data point supporting continuation, but it does not independently validate the original diagnosis. Stimulants produce subjective focus and executive-function benefits in many conditions and in some people without a formal ADHD diagnosis; ~20% of prescription-stimulant misusers exaggerate symptoms.[ref:aafp-2024][ref:nejm-volkow2013] Treat the stable course as supportive evidence for ongoing benefit, not as proof the original work-up was correct.

That said, the question for a primary-care provider is usually "should continuation continue?", not "was the original diagnosis valid?" — and on that question, the long-term evidence supports continuing if the patient is stable and functional. A randomized placebo-controlled discontinuation study after 2+ years of methylphenidate found significant worsening on discontinuation (ADHD-RS −4.6, 95% CI −8.7 to −0.56), confirming that long-term efficacy holds for adults who respond.[ref:matthijssen-ajp-2019][ref:rosenau-ecap-2025] Real-world retention data show 30–40% of adult patients still on stimulants at 5 years (with reinitiation), and major guidelines frame the appropriate periodic check-in as "continue versus stop," not "re-diagnose."[ref:brikell-lancet-2024][ref:aacap-greenhill2002]

Practical triage: a long-stable patient with no red flags and a thin chart is a lower priority for formal re-evaluation than a recent diagnosis, a request to escalate dose, or emerging behavioral concerns. Document your clinical reasoning. If at any point continuation feels uncomfortable, an e-consult is the right path.

faqs.title: Ceiling doses and recent escalations

items.question: What are the ceiling doses for common stimulants?
items.answer_html:
FDA maximum daily doses are formulation-specific; blanket numbers across a stimulant class are misleading and have led to clinical errors. Verify against the specific product label before flagging a patient as exceeding maximum dose.

Amphetamine salts (Adderall) — IR tablets FDA-labeled adult max 40 mg/day; the label states that only in rare cases is it necessary to exceed 40 mg/day.[ref:fda-adderall-ir][ref:cochrane-castells2018]

Amphetamine salts (Adderall XR) — extended-release capsules Label-recommended adult dose 20 mg/day; doses up to 60 mg/day were studied in clinical trials but without evidence of additional benefit beyond 20 mg/day.[ref:fda-adderall-xr] The evidence-supported ceiling for the XR formulation is therefore considerably lower than the studied range.

Methylphenidate IR / SR / most ER (non-Concerta) FDA-labeled adult max 60 mg/day.[ref:fda-methylphenidate]

Methylphenidate (Concerta) — OROS extended-release FDA-labeled adult max 72 mg/day. Concerta has its own ceiling distinct from other methylphenidate products; a patient on Concerta 72 mg is at FDA maximum, not exceeding it.[ref:fda-concerta]

Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) FDA-labeled adult max 70 mg/day. The 70 mg ceiling is a regulatory maximum, not a pharmacologic ceiling inherent to the prodrug. The prodrug design reduces abuse potential by requiring enzymatic activation but does not create a kinetic plateau that prevents higher doses from acting.[ref:fda-vyvanse][ref:jama-psych-farhat2024] Renal dose adjustments: 50 mg/day for severe renal impairment; 30 mg/day for ESRD.[ref:fda-vyvanse]

What the dose-response evidence says about "more is better" A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of licensed and unlicensed stimulant doses for adult ADHD (Farhat 2024) found:

For amphetamines, the symptom-reduction curve plateaus at roughly 30–35 mg/day (ED95 ≈ 30 mg/day). Doses above the FDA license offer no detectable additional symptom benefit — "unlicensed" doses are not benign, just unhelpful.[ref:jama-psych-farhat2024]

For methylphenidate, ED95 ≈ 72.5 mg/day — meaning the Concerta ceiling at 72 mg is well-calibrated to the evidence-based dose-response curve. Doses above 60 mg/day continue to deliver small incremental symptom gains, but adverse-event–driven dropout roughly doubles (OR ≈ 2.02 above license).[ref:jama-psych-farhat2024][ref:cochrane-candido2021]

Documentation thresholds (formulation-specific) Document explicit clinical rationale for: amphetamine IR > 40 mg/day (already at FDA ceiling), Adderall XR > 20 mg/day (above evidence-supported dose, even if within the studied range), and methylphenidate or Concerta at maximum with continued symptom or function gaps. AACAP guidance is that any dose above the standard maximum should be accompanied by documentation that lower doses were inadequate and that higher doses are not producing adverse effects.[ref:aacap-greenhill2002][ref:fda-adderall-xr][ref:fda-adderall-ir]

Doses above the FDA-labeled maximum for each formulation are outside this framework and require specialist co-management.

items.question: The patient was escalated to max dose by the prior provider. Do I continue?
items.answer_html:
Continuing a maximum-dose prescription is within primary care scope if it's clinically justified and documented. The burden of documentation is higher at the ceiling than at moderate doses.

At first visit: review the chart for the rationale behind escalation. If it's documented and coherent — continue with your own documented review.

If there's no documented rationale for the ceiling dose — or if the escalation happened recently and rapidly — this is an e-consult trigger. The question for psychiatry: "Patient is at maximum dose of [medication] without clear documented rationale. Please review current plan and advise whether to maintain, taper, or restructure."

faqs.title: When function declines despite medication

items.question: What counts as a "behavioral red flag"?
items.answer_html:
Behavioral red flags are signs that the medication may be causing harm, being misused, or masking an underlying condition that is worsening:

Mood instability — new or worsening irritability, emotional dysregulation, or rage that the patient or family attributes to medication timing.

Sleep disruption severe enough to impair function — beyond expected stimulant effect, especially if the patient is escalating to cope.

Increasing psychological dependence — patient describes inability to function at all without the medication in ways that feel qualitatively different from therapeutic benefit.

Cardiovascular monitoring is its own structured workstream — not just a red-flag question. Across treated patients, all ADHD medications (stimulants and most nonstimulants) produce small but real increases in blood pressure and pulse, and 5–15% of patients show substantial outlier responses well beyond the group mean — which is the evidence-based reason to monitor every patient on therapy, not only those with symptoms.[ref:lancet-psych-farhat2025][ref:fda-adderall-xr][ref:aap-wolraich2019][ref:jamaopen-oliva2025]

Baseline screening (before continuing or initiating)

BP and pulse — use AHA/ACC hypertension staging; there is no ADHD-specific cutoff. Stage 1 (130–139 / 80–89): monitor closely. Stage 2 (≥140/90): defer dose escalation or initiation until controlled. Hypertensive crisis (≥180/120): absolute contraindication. FDA labels contraindicate stimulants in moderate-to-severe hypertension.[ref:aafp-2024][ref:fda-adderall-xr][ref:jacc-torresacosta2020]

ECG is not routinely required for an adult starting or continuing stimulants. Obtain only when personal or family history, or examination, suggests cardiac disease.[ref:aafp-2024][ref:fda-adderall-xr][ref:lancet-thapar2016][ref:aap-wolraich2019]

Personal cardiac history triggering pre-prescribing cardiology workup: structural heart disease, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, coronary artery disease, prior MI, or Wolff-Parkinson-White. Family history triggers: sudden cardiac death, ventricular arrhythmia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome. Symptom triggers: exertional chest pain, unexplained syncope, exertional dyspnea, palpitations.[ref:fda-adderall-xr][ref:aap-wolraich2019][ref:ecap-lee2026][ref:amssm-putukian2011]

Ongoing monitoring cadence

Baseline + after each dose change + at minimum every 6 months for stable patients on continuing therapy; every 3 months for patients with cardiovascular risk factors or borderline readings.[ref:nejm-cortese2020][ref:fda-adderall-xr][ref:nejm-volkow2013] Weight is a guideline-specified monitoring element at the same 6-month cadence in adults.[ref:nejm-cortese2020]

Action thresholds Sustained resting heart rate >120 bpm, or systolic blood pressure consistently ≥140/90 on two separate occasions, warrant dose reduction and specialist referral. These thresholds derive primarily from NICE / European ADHD Guidelines Group expert consensus and are pediatric-derived, extrapolated to adults — not US-guideline-graded for the adult population.[ref:nejm-cortese2020]

ABPM 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is not standard ADHD monitoring. It can be useful selectively for equivocal office readings (distinguishing stimulant-attributable from white-coat hypertension); the evidence base is limited.[ref:jch-cluett2021][ref:eneuropsych-buitelaar2022]

Long-term cardiovascular risk A large Swedish nested case-control study (Zhang 2024, n≈278,000, 14-year follow-up) found a small but real incremental cardiovascular risk during the first ~3 years of stimulant exposure (~4% increased CVD risk per year of exposure), then a plateau; >5-year exposure adjusted OR 1.23 (95% CI 1.12–1.36). The signal was driven by hypertension (AOR 1.80) and arterial disease (AOR 1.65); there was no increased risk of arrhythmia, heart failure, ischemic heart disease, or stroke. Risk became significant only at ≥1.5× defined daily dose (e.g., methylphenidate ≥45 mg/day).[ref:jama-psych-zhang2024][ref:jacc-holt2024][ref:jamaopen-zhang2022] The data are observational and cannot establish causation, but support patient counseling on "modest incremental cardiovascular risk, primarily blood-pressure-mediated, dose-dependent."

Switching to a nonstimulant does not eliminate the cardiovascular question Atomoxetine and viloxazine produce blood-pressure and heart-rate effects of comparable magnitude to stimulants in network meta-analysis; switching for cardiovascular concerns alone is generally not justified.[ref:lancet-psych-farhat2025][ref:jamaopen-oliva2025] Guanfacine is the only ADHD agent associated with decreased blood pressure and pulse (adult mean changes: SBP −10.1 mmHg, DBP −7.73 mmHg, HR −6.83 bpm) — a potential option when cardiovascular concerns limit stimulant continuation, though it is generally outside an inherited-stimulant continuation discussion and may warrant specialist input.[ref:lancet-psych-farhat2025]

Evidence limit to disclose No RCT cardiovascular data exist beyond ~52 weeks of treatment; only 4 RCTs reach 24 weeks. All long-term ADHD cardiovascular evidence is observational.[ref:lancet-psych-farhat2025]

Acute cardiovascular symptoms at current dose Palpitations, chest pain, exertional symptoms, syncope, or unexplained dyspnea warrant immediate dose reassessment, ECG and cardiology consultation as indicated, and consideration of therapy change rather than dose escalation.[ref:lancet-psych-farhat2025][ref:aafp-2024][ref:nejm-cortese2020]

items.question: Could this be something other than ADHD at this point?
items.answer_html:
Comorbidity in adult ADHD is the rule, not the exception. Adults with ADHD carry markedly elevated odds of mood, anxiety, and substance-use disorders (ORs in the 4.5–8.7 range across the major categories), and ADHD/PTSD comorbidity is reported at 28–36% in adult cohorts.[ref:hartman-nbr-2023][ref:magdi-sysrev-2025] So the right question is rarely "ADHD or something else?" and is usually "ADHD plus what?"

The DSM-5-TR differential rests on temporal pattern: ADHD is persistent with developmental onset (symptoms before age 12) versus the episodic course of bipolar disorder, the worry-driven cognition of anxiety disorders, and the trauma-linked hypervigilance of PTSD.[ref:dsm-5-tr-2022][ref:aafp-2024]

The older clinical convention that stimulants reliably worsen anxiety, mania, or hyperarousal is not well supported by current evidence:

Anxiety — Population-level data run the opposite direction. A pediatric meta-analysis (23 RCTs, n≈3,000) found stimulants reduced treatment-emergent anxiety (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.77–0.95).[ref:coughlin-jcap-2015][ref:golubchik-icp-2021] Adult safety meta-analyses are consistent — net effect on anxiety is neutral to favorable, not harmful.[ref:jamaopen-oliva2025] A minority of patients do worsen, but stimulants remain first-line even with comorbid anxiety.

Bipolar disorder — The clinically actionable distinction is monotherapy versus stimulant + mood stabilizer, not bipolar I versus II. In a Swedish registry of adults with bipolar disorder (n=2,307), methylphenidate monotherapy was associated with HR 6.7 for treatment-emergent mania, whereas methylphenidate with a mood stabilizer was associated with HR 0.6 — a reduction.[ref:viktorin-ajp-2017][ref:jefsen-jcp-2023][ref:chiorean-bd-2024] FDA labels carry a class warning for bipolar disorder; causality remains very-low-GRADE evidence.[ref:salazar-jamapsych-2025] If you suspect undiagnosed or undertreated bipolar disorder, stabilize the mood disorder first; don't simply stop the stimulant.

PTSD — The "stimulants worsen hyperarousal" framing is clinical convention without controlled-trial support. Emerging real-world youth data (n>714,000 ADHD, ~30,000 with comorbid PTSD) found stimulant treatment associated with the most favorable outcomes across hospitalizations, ED visits, and antipsychotic/mood-stabilizer use (adjusted HRs 0.52–0.74); clinicians appear to under-prescribe stimulants in this population despite superior outcomes.[ref:baweja-jad-2026][ref:magdi-sysrev-2025] Adult-population data are thinner, so monitor for hyperarousal — but do not reflexively discontinue.

If a patient is deteriorating on stimulants, the right move is psychiatric input framed around comorbidity management — what to add, taper, or sequence — rather than a unilateral discontinuation. The e-consult question should name the specific comorbidity concern.

faqs.title: Patient requesting combination or second stimulant

items.question: Is combination stimulant therapy ever appropriate?
items.answer_html:
Yes — and the original module framing that combination stimulant therapy is "outside the scope of primary care" imports a UK NICE specialist-gatekeeping model into a US context where guidelines say something different. No US guideline (AAP, AAFP, AACAP, APA) restricts same-class IR booster prescribing to specialists.[ref:aap-wolraich2019][ref:aafp-2024][ref:aacap-greenhill2002][ref:nice-ng87][ref:bjgp-price2024][ref:bmc-asherson2022] AAP explicitly tasks the primary-care clinician with stimulant titration including formulation choice, and ≥90% of patients respond when a range of doses and formulations are tried.[ref:aap-wolraich2019][ref:chang-aafp-2020] Cortese 2021 frames the same-class long-acting + short-acting booster as a routine end-of-dose-wearing-off strategy, not specialist-only territory.[ref:cortese-cns-2021]

Definitional clarity "Polypharmacy" in the ADHD literature is reserved for cross-class combinations — for example, a stimulant plus an alpha-agonist, atomoxetine, or SSRI. A long-acting methylphenidate plus an IR methylphenidate booster (or a long-acting amphetamine plus an IR dextroamphetamine booster) is same-class formulation optimization, not polypharmacy.[ref:baker-jcap-2021][ref:cortese-cns-2021] Cross-class combinations (e.g., amphetamine + methylphenidate) are uncommon and warrant specialist justification; same-class long-acting + booster does not, on its own.

The honest guardrail is competency-based, not scope-based: am I comfortable managing this combination?, not am I allowed to manage this combination? If a patient arrives already on a multi-agent regimen and the prescribing rationale is unclear or you are unfamiliar with combination dosing, specialist consultation is reasonable — but it is not a regulatory or guideline-mandated requirement.

items.question: The patient is asking me to add a booster dose to their existing medication.
items.answer_html:
Adding a short-acting same-class booster to a long-acting regimen — methylphenidate IR added to a methylphenidate ER product, or dextroamphetamine IR added to lisdexamfetamine — is a routine titration strategy for end-of-dose wearing off, not specialist-only territory in the US.[ref:cortese-cns-2021][ref:aap-wolraich2019][ref:aafp-2024][ref:aacap-greenhill2002] The original framing that this requires psychiatry sign-off in primary care is not consistent with US guidelines.

The honest version of the guardrail: am I comfortable with the combination dosing math, the cumulative ceiling, and the side-effect monitoring this entails? If yes, continue or initiate the booster with documentation of the rationale (end-of-dose wearing off, functional gap in afternoon coverage, etc.) and the cumulative daily dose check against the FDA ceiling for that class. If you are unfamiliar with combination dosing, specialist consultation is a reasonable choice — but it is a competency call, not a scope mandate.[ref:aafp-2024][ref:cortese-cns-2021]

Conversation with the patient: "A short-acting booster on top of your long-acting medication is a routine option for end-of-dose coverage. I want to confirm we stay within the cumulative dose limit and watch for side effects on the afternoon dose; let's plan a check-in at [interval]."

Cross-class combination Adding a different stimulant class (amphetamine plus methylphenidate, or stimulant plus alpha-agonist or atomoxetine) is uncommon, less well-characterized, and a reasonable trigger for specialist input.[ref:baker-jcap-2021][ref:cortese-cns-2021]

items.question: The patient had a booster dose prescribed before and wants to restart it.
items.answer_html:
Restarting a previously prescribed regimen is generally lower-risk than initiating something new, but treat that as clinical convention rather than a guideline-graded distinction; no US ADHD guideline formally addresses the restart-versus-initiate question.[ref:aacap-greenhill2002]

The supportive factors: prior documentation in the chart, PDMP confirmation that the regimen was previously dispensed and tolerated, and a non-clinical reason for the original discontinuation (provider change, insurance disruption). Caveats that matter: prior tolerability does not guarantee current safety; gap duration matters (cardiovascular and psychiatric status can shift); and documentation quality matters (PDMP and pharmacy records weigh more than patient self-report alone). Reassess current blood pressure, heart rate, and psychiatric status before restarting.[ref:lancet-psych-farhat2025][ref:aafp-2024]

If the prior prescribing record shows the combination was used, was safe, and was discontinued for a non-clinical reason, continuation with fresh documentation is defensible. If gaps in the record or in the clinical picture are open, an e-consult is always available — that is the framework doing its job, not a failure.
