modules.landing_intro: A patient is transferring to your panel on a chronic opiate regimen. This is one of the highest-anxiety handoffs in primary care — and one of the most common. Your job at the first visit is not to solve the problem. It is to establish the relationship, complete a structured assessment, and determine whether you can continue, need to modify, or need to escalate. Do not discontinue at the first visit without a safety plan in place. The CDC 2022 guideline (Recommendation 5) is explicit that opioid therapy should not be discontinued abruptly and that clinicians should not rapidly reduce opioid dosages from higher dosages, except when there are life-threatening safety signals; abrupt taper of long-stable patients is associated with overdose, mental-health crisis, and suicide attempt.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:agnoli-jama-2021][ref:aafp-roth-2020]
modules.checklist_section_label: Before you decide — verify all four

checklist.statement: PDMP reviewed — single prescriber, single pharmacy, consistent quantities, no concurrent controlled substances of concern
Controlled substance agreement on file or completed at this visit — patient understands monitoring expectations
Urine drug screen obtained at intake — results reviewed and documented
Current MME calculated — dose is documented and clinical rationale is present for doses ≥ 50 MME/day (the CDC 2022 reassessment guidepost)

green_zone.zone_label: All boxes checked — Continue with monitoring
green_zone.narrative_html: Reasonable basis to continue current regimen at this visit, anchored in CDC 2022 Recommendations 2, 5, 7, 8, and 9 for patients on long-term opioid therapy.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023] Document using SmartPhrase below. Schedule follow-up at 90 days or sooner if any concerns emerge. Monitoring is ongoing — this is not a one-time clearance. The compact 4-item checklist above captures the at-the-moment go/no-go; the broader 11-element CDC-aligned first-visit framework (continue absent life-threatening signals; PDMP per state; UDS as baseline; offer naloxone; OUD screen; PEG functional assessment; concurrent-benzo check; treatment goals; documentation rationale; pain-management consult if function not improving / docs limited / dose well above 50 MME without justification; 1–3 month follow-up) lives in the FAQ surface as supplementary guidance.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:coffin-am-2022][ref:sandbrink-aim-2023] You are institutionally supported.

escalation.statement: Current dose well above the 50 MME/day reassessment guidepost without clear documented benefit; risk increases continuously with dose, and the CDC 2022 guideline does not specify a single numeric ceiling
Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription — particular caution warranted (CDC 2022 Recommendation 11, Category B); does not require automatic discontinuation
UDS positive for non-prescribed controlled substance, or unexpectedly negative for the prescribed opiate (apply the full differential before drawing conclusions)
PDMP shows multiple prescribers, multiple pharmacies, or overlapping fills — pattern warrants clarification with the patient and other prescribers, not assumption of diversion

Repeated early refill requests, lost medications, or escalating contact between visits — apply differential dx (undertreated pain, psychiatric comorbidity, social stressors, OUD) before assuming misuse
Any clinical concern for opioid use disorder — apply DSM-5 11-criterion checklist with pain-adjusted approach and consider MOUD rather than taper or discontinuation

context_strip.label: National context
context_strip.text: This module supports the primary care provider at the inherited-patient first visit and synthesizes the CDC 2022 opioid prescribing guideline, the ASAM/ACMT 2025 benzodiazepine tapering guideline, the VA/DoD 2022 chronic-pain guideline, and AAFP commentary; no single national source packages this scenario as a unified protocol.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:vadod-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023][ref:coffin-am-2022] Numeric thresholds referenced in the module — early-refill ladders, UDS cadence tiers, '3 pharmacies' as a heuristic — reflect institutional convention informed by AAPM/APS expert consensus rather than specific CDC recommendations; the CDC 2022 guideline deliberately avoids rigid numeric thresholds and explicitly declines to recommend risk-stratified UDS cadence.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aapm-argoff-2018][ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009] Regulatory prose covers New York and New Jersey explicitly because the two states' PDMP duty-to-consult structures differ materially.[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1]

modules.footer_note: For internal use only. This is a viable first pathway, not the only pathway. Experienced providers retain clinical discretion. The module's intake checklist is intentionally compact for at-the-moment decisioning; the broader 11-element CDC-2022-aligned first-visit framework lives in the FAQ surface as supplementary guidance. Regulatory prose covers New York and New Jersey explicitly (PDMP rules differ between the two states); providers in other jurisdictions should verify their state's controlled-substance requirements with their compliance office. Numeric thresholds referenced in this module — early-refill ladders, UDS cadence tiers, '3 pharmacies' as a heuristic — reflect institutional convention informed by expert consensus rather than specific guideline thresholds; the CDC 2022 guideline deliberately avoids rigid numeric thresholds. Verify current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

faqs.title: What am I looking for in the PDMP for opiate patients?

items.question: How is the opiate PDMP review different from stimulants?
items.answer_html:
The patterns to look for are co-equal top safety concerns rather than a single most-important flag. Per CDC 2022 (Recommendation 9), high total MME/day, dangerous combinations, and prescriptions from multiple uncoordinated clinicians are co-equal triggers for safety action; concurrent opioid–benzodiazepine prescribing is one of the top concerns, not the only one.[ref:cdc-2022]

Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription Document a risk-benefit assessment. The combination is associated with roughly a 2–5× increase in overdose-related outcomes depending on population, dose, and duration; risk is highest in the early period of concurrent use and declines after 180 days of stable concurrent use.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:fda-oxycodone][ref:hernandez-jamaopen-2018][ref:sun-bmj-2017] CDC 2022 Recommendation 11 is Category B ("particular caution"), not Category A ("avoid") — long-term stable use may be safer than abrupt discontinuation.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo]

Overlapping fills from any prescriber The pattern warrants clarification and documentation, not the presumption of "double-doctoring." CDC 2022 explicitly notes that prescriptions may appropriately be written by more than one clinician coordinating care, and PDMP information can be incorrect (wrong name, identity theft).[ref:cdc-2022] The recommended response is to discuss findings with the patient, confirm awareness, and communicate with other prescribers.[ref:cdc-2022]

Fill frequency vs days supply A pattern of consistently early fills (e.g., a 30-day supply filled every 20 days) is more concerning than an isolated occurrence — Kern 2020 found that ~10% of opioid patients have an early fill (≥15% early relative to days' supply), and 75% of those patients have only one. Distinguish pattern from one-off; legitimate explanations include vacation prep, dose adjustments, and 14-day refills written as 30-day supply.[ref:kern-pm-2020][ref:liebschutz-jamaim-2017][ref:babu-nejm-2019]

Cash-pay fills PDMPs are pharmacy-based reporting systems, not insurance-based — pharmacies are required to report all dispensed controlled substances to the PDMP regardless of payment method in virtually all states, so cash-pay fills do appear on the PDMP.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:manasco-pds-2016] The clinically meaningful concern is cash payment for controlled substances by a patient who has active insurance — this can indicate an attempt to circumvent insurance quantity limits or prior authorization, and is worth asking about. PDMP reporting lag varies by state (most are now next-business-day or real-time).[ref:manasco-pds-2016]

Algorithmic risk scores PDMP-generated risk scores have not been validated against clinical outcomes and should not replace clinical judgment; the CDC warns that they can lead to stigmatization and may disparately affect women, persons of color, and persons living in poverty.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:perry-add-2022] A 10-year longitudinal analysis found that traditional binary thresholds (N+ unique doctors and N+ unique pharmacies in 90 days) performed no better than chance at predicting OUD or overdose after 2015.[ref:perry-add-2022] CDC 2022 is also explicit: clinicians should not dismiss patients from practice on the basis of PDMP information.[ref:cdc-2022]

New York Under NY Public Health Law §3343-a (I-STOP), every practitioner must consult the PMP registry prior to prescribing or dispensing any Schedule II, III, or IV controlled substance; Schedule V is not covered by the duty to consult.[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:istop-blum2016][ref:istop-virani2018] Statutory exceptions: veterinarians, on-premises institutional dispensing (§3342), administering (vs prescribing), ED prescribing of ≤5-day supply, hospice patients (§4002), and certain technical-failure or waiver situations.[ref:ny-pbh-3343a]

New Jersey Under NJSA 45:1-46.1 (P.L.2017 c.341), NJ PMP access is required at three trigger points: (a) first-time prescription of a Schedule II controlled substance or any opioid for acute or chronic pain to a new patient; (b) first-time prescription of a Schedule III/IV benzodiazepine to a new patient; and (c) quarterly during the period the patient continues to receive such prescriptions.[ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1] NJ's per-prescription consultation duty is narrower than New York's — initial plus quarterly is the operational standard for ongoing therapy in NJ.

Verify current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

items.question: I see a second prescriber in the PDMP. Is that automatically a problem?
items.answer_html:
Not automatically — and the framing should be "warrants clarification," not "suggests diversion." CDC 2022 explicitly states that prescriptions may appropriately be written by more than one clinician coordinating the patient's care.[ref:cdc-2022] A patient seeing both a PCP and a pain-management specialist may have legitimate dual prescribing if it is coordinated; an ER prescription for an acute injury is qualitatively different from a pattern of monthly fills from two separate primary care offices.[ref:cdc-2022]

Ask the patient directly, document what they tell you, and contact the other prescriber if the answer is unclear. The documentation requirement is evidence of coordination — a note or communication confirming that both prescribers are aware of each other's prescribing and have agreed on a care plan.[ref:cdc-2022] Avoid the term "double-doctoring" in clinical documentation until the pattern is confirmed as uncoordinated.

items.question: What do I do if I find a concurrent benzo prescription?
items.answer_html:
The CDC 2022 guideline (Recommendation 11) is a Category B recommendation — "particular caution," not "avoid" — and explicitly acknowledges that stopping benzodiazepines can be destabilizing and that long-term stable use may be safer than erratic, unpredictable use.[ref:cdc-2022] Refusing to prescribe one or both at the first visit risks destabilizing the patient and is explicitly cautioned against by the CDC OWG.[ref:cdc-2022]

The first-visit pattern is bridge both, document, and refer:[ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo]

(1) Continue both medications at current doses if the patient is on a long-term, stable regimen. (2) Document the combination as a known risk and the risk-benefit assessment (dose, duration, indication, prior taper attempts, functional status, prior overdose, household risk).[ref:cdc-2022] (3) Prescribe naloxone — ASAM 2025 makes this a strong recommendation for all patients co-prescribed opioids and benzodiazepines.[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo] (4) Check the PDMP. (5) Plan a shorter-interval follow-up (2–4 weeks rather than 3 months) given the higher-risk regimen.[ref:cdc-2022] (6) Initiate (not necessarily complete) specialist referral if there is concern about indication or if tapering is being considered.[ref:cdc-2022] See the escalation FAQ for the full opioid–benzo workflow.

faqs.title: The CS agreement — what it is and what it isn't

items.question: Do I need a new agreement if the prior provider had one on file?
items.answer_html:
A new agreement on prescriber-of-record transfer is strongly recommended best practice and often legally required, though not a universal national mandate.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aan-franklin-2014][ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009] CDC 2022 specifically addresses inherited patients: clinicians seeing new patients already using opioid medication should establish treatment goals (including functional goals) and clearly document a treatment plan.[ref:cdc-2022] A 2024 legal landscape review found that 27 states mandate Opioid Treatment Agreements with substantial variation in mandated terms; 23 states plus DC do not mandate by statute.[ref:svirsky-milbank-2024]

The rationale for a new agreement on transfer is sound: the prior agreement was between the patient and a different clinician — it does not bind the new prescriber; documentation of a new agreement protects the incoming clinician in both civil and criminal litigation; and reviewing it at the first visit is a clinical moment, not just a signature exercise (it gives you a chance to assess patient understanding and signals a managed relationship).[ref:cdc-2022][ref:laks-jgim-2021][ref:bruce-cid-2017]

New York NY I-STOP mandates PDMP checks before prescribing controlled substances but does not independently mandate a written OTA by statute.[ref:istop-blum2016][ref:istop-virani2018] The OTA requirement in NY typically derives from institutional policy or health-system standards. Verify your institution's specific policy.

New Jersey No NJ statute independently mandates a written OTA; institutional policy is the operational standard.[ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1] Verify with your compliance office.

Verify current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

items.question: What should the agreement cover?
items.answer_html:
These are consensus-derived common elements consistent with best practice drawn from CDC 2022, APS/AAPM 2009, ACOEM, and HIVMA/IDSA — not a nationally standardized required-element list. The CDC 2022 guideline explicitly avoided specifying OTA content and noted that "clinical evidence reviews did not find studies evaluating the effectiveness of written agreements or treatment plans"; APS/AAPM said "there is insufficient evidence to guide specific recommendations on which provisions to include."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009][ref:bruce-cid-2017][ref:hegmann-joem-2014][ref:acoem-2017-otc][ref:nuckols-aim-2014]

Common elements with provenance notes:

Single prescriber, single pharmacy Reasonable risk-mitigation provisions; not federally mandated. CDC 2022 intentionally moved away from rigid rules.[ref:cdc-2022]

UDS monitoring CDC 2022 softened the 2016 language to "as appropriate" rather than mandating universal testing.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023]

No early refills, no patient self-adjustment of dose Reasonable and widely included; not guideline-specified at the element level.

No replacement for lost or stolen medications Common institutional risk-management policy, not federal regulation. Federal law does not categorically prohibit replacement (see the behavior FAQ).[ref:cfr-1306-04][ref:asam-risk2024]

Functional improvement as the primary goal The element with the strongest guideline backing. CDC 2022: "Emphasize improvement in function as a primary goal and that function can improve even when pain is not eliminated."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:cdc-2016] Both 2016 and 2022 guidelines define clinically meaningful improvement as a 30% improvement in scores for both pain and function using tools such as the PEG scale (Pain, Enjoyment, General activity).[ref:cdc-2022][ref:cdc-2016]

Carve-out CDC 2022 acknowledges that "for some patients with diseases typically associated with progressive functional impairment or catastrophic injuries such as spinal cord trauma, reductions in pain without improvement in physical function might be more realistic."[ref:cdc-2022] Don't rigidly apply the functional-improvement frame to all patients.

SmartPhrase .CSAGREE populates the standard institutional template. The label on whatever you use should read "consensus-derived common elements," not "required elements."

items.question: The patient refuses to sign. What do I do?
items.answer_html:
A patient who refuses to sign is communicating something worth understanding before you respond. Ask why; explore literacy or language barriers, prior negative experiences, or simply needing time to read. Refusing to prescribe without a signed agreement is defensible — but the CDC 2022 guideline also warns explicitly against patient abandonment: "Clinicians should avoid dismissing patients from care and should ensure (provide or arrange) appropriate care for patients with pain."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009]

The chart documentation should reflect a four-element pattern that protects both the patient and the clinician:

(1) The agreement was offered and explained, with accommodations as needed (literacy assistance, language interpretation, time to review).[ref:beck-jme-2021] (2) The patient declined to sign, with the patient's stated reason if any. (3) The clinician offered alternatives — non-opioid pain management, referral to a pain specialist, a bridge prescription with short-interval follow-up. (4) The rationale for not prescribing the chronic opioid without the agreement.[ref:cdc-2022]

You are not obligated to prescribe without a signed agreement, and the institutional framework supports that position — but the documentation must show that you offered alternatives, not that you terminated the relationship.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:svirsky-milbank-2024]

faqs.title: UDS at intake — interpreting and acting on results

items.question: What is the difference between a screening UDS and a confirmatory test?
items.answer_html:
The point-of-care immunoassay (the cup test) is a screen — it has meaningful false-positive and false-negative rates. CDC 2022 (Recommendation 10) states that "false positive and false negative presumptive results are not uncommon" and that this problem is compounded because clinicians commonly misinterpret results.[ref:cdc-2022] Analytically, POC immunoassays can have positive predictive values as low as 57% for oxycodone and poor negative predictive values for several drug classes (25–29% for THC-COOH).[ref:abou-cb-2021] All immunoassay results are presumptive until confirmatory testing.[ref:saitman-jat-2026][ref:kale-aafp-2019]

A positive screen for an unexpected substance, or an unexpected negative for the prescribed opiate, should be confirmed with GC-MS or LC-MS/MS when the result will inform decisions with major clinical implications.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:asam-baxter-2017][ref:stolbach-jmt-2022] POC results can appropriately inform preliminary safety steps such as withholding a same-day prescription pending confirmation, increasing monitoring frequency, or initiating a clinical conversation — these are not "actions against" the patient.[ref:mahajan-aa-2017]

The CDC position is broader than "confirm before adverse action": even confirmed unexpected results should not trigger dismissal from care. Confirmed findings should prompt a clinical response — MOUD evaluation, increased monitoring, naloxone, referral — not termination.[ref:cdc-2022]

A useful pre-test framing per AAPM consensus: ask the patient before sending the test, "If we test you today, what will we find in your urine? Will there be any surprises?" A candid answer can sometimes obviate the need for confirmatory testing on that visit.[ref:aapm-argoff-2018][ref:cdc-2022]

items.question: The UDS is negative for the prescribed opiate. What does that mean?
items.answer_html:
The differential is broader than three items. Document consideration of the full set before drawing conclusions:[ref:alford-jama-2013][ref:cdc-2022][ref:bruce-cid-2017][ref:aapm-argoff-2018][ref:stolbach-jmt-2022]

Wrong assay ordered The single most operationally important addition. The standard "opiate" immunoassay does not detect oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, or buprenorphine; a chronic oxycodone patient can show "no opiates detected" on a routine cup test that would be entirely expected. Verify the assay panel detects the prescribed agent before drawing conclusions.[ref:alford-jama-2013][ref:stolbach-jmt-2022]

Running out early due to undertreated pain The patient used more than prescribed and has none left at testing — distinct from diversion and clinically actionable (suggests dose may be inadequate or PRN guidance unclear).[ref:bruce-cid-2017][ref:alford-jama-2013]

Drug absent (used > 72 hours ago) Diversion, hoarding/stockpiling, or pharmacologic induction causing rapid metabolism.[ref:alford-jama-2013]

Drug present but below assay cutoff Dose-timing artifact (less common with chronic dosing) or low-dose / PRN use patterns.[ref:alford-jama-2013][ref:nccn-cancer-pain-2026]

Specimen manipulation Dilution, adulteration, or substitution of synthetic urine.[ref:alford-jama-2013]

Urine dilution from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus A real metabolic confound.[ref:bruce-cid-2017]

Pharmacogenetic anomalies and drug-drug interactions Affecting metabolism of the prescribed agent.[ref:aapm-argoff-2018]

Laboratory error Mislabeling, cross-reaction causing interference.[ref:alford-jama-2013]

Confirm with send-out testing where confirmation will change management. Have a non-accusatory conversation: "I want to make sure we understand this result together before drawing any conclusions."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aapm-argoff-2018] Document the conversation and the plan for follow-up testing.

items.question: How often should UDS be repeated after intake?
items.answer_html:
The cadence below is institutional convention informed by AAPM and APS expert consensus, not a specific CDC recommendation. CDC 2022 deliberately declined to recommend risk-stratified UDS frequency, noting that "predicting risk is challenging, and available tools do not allow clinicians to reliably identify patients who are at low risk."[ref:cdc-2022] CDC's only direct recommendation is "periodically (at least annually)."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aapm-argoff-2018][ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009]

UDS should also be treated as baseline monitoring for chronic-opiate patients, not as a punitive trigger pulled only when behavioral concerns surface.[ref:cdc-2016][ref:cdc-2022][ref:jannetto-jalm-2018]

Stable patient (clean PDMP, signed agreement, no behavioral concerns) — every 6–12 months is a defensible institutional standard. AAPM 2018 consensus: every 6 months to 2 years for low-risk.[ref:aapm-argoff-2018]

Yellow flags — every 3 months. AAPM consensus: 1–3 times per year for moderate risk.[ref:aapm-argoff-2018]

Active concerns or recent escalation — at every visit until stable. This tier is more aggressive than published guidelines (which typically suggest 2–4 times per year, with "weekly for very high risk" per APS); keep it as institutional choice and document the rationale for the chosen interval.[ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009][ref:aapm-argoff-2018][ref:cdc-2022]

Document your reasoning for the interval chosen at the time you choose it — CMS and payer policies require documentation of medical necessity for definitive testing.[ref:aapm-argoff-2018]

faqs.title: Morphine milligram equivalents — calculating and contextualizing

items.question: How do I calculate MME?
items.answer_html:
Multiply the daily dose by the CDC 2022 conversion factor for that opioid. The CDC notes there is "no single standard formula for calculating MMEs"; institutional variation exists, and these factors are estimates.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:wen-jpm-2022]

Morphine — 1:1 (30 mg morphine = 30 MME)[ref:cdc-2022]

Oxycodone — × 1.5 (30 mg oxycodone = 45 MME)[ref:cdc-2022]

Hydrocodone — × 1 (30 mg hydrocodone = 30 MME)[ref:cdc-2022]

Hydromorphone — × 5 (8 mg hydromorphone = 40 MME). Note: the 2016 CDC table used 4.0 and there is significant institutional variation in hydromorphone conversion factors.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:cdc-2016][ref:wen-jpm-2022]

Fentanyl patch — mcg/hr × 2.4 (25 mcg/hr patch = 60 MME/day)[ref:cdc-2022]

Tramadol — × 0.2 per CDC 2022 (200 mg tramadol = 40 MME). Some institutional tables use 0.1 — that is incorrect at the federal-guideline level and underestimates MME by half. Tramadol is a dual-mechanism agent (µ-receptor agonist + serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), and it is unknown whether tramadol is associated with overdose in the same dose-dependent manner as pure µ-agonists.[ref:cdc-2022]

Methadone — × 4.7 per CDC 2022, but with a highly variable and dose-dependent conversion. Methadone requires special caution due to its long, variable half-life; conversion factors are estimates and can mislead at higher doses.[ref:cdc-2022]

Tapentadol — × 0.4[ref:cdc-2022]

Buprenorphine — exclude from MME summation Buprenorphine should not be counted in total MME calculations because of its partial-agonist properties and ceiling effect on respiratory depression. MME conversion factors should also not be applied to methadone or buprenorphine when used for opioid use disorder treatment.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:asam-2021-moud]

For patients on multiple non-buprenorphine opiates, sum the per-agent MMEs.[ref:cdc-2022]

items.question: What are the thresholds I should know?
items.answer_html:
CDC 2022 frames overdose risk as continuous with dose, with no single safe threshold. The 2022 guideline deliberately removed specific dosage thresholds from the main recommendation statement, citing concern that "specific dosage thresholds in a main recommendation statement would emphasize them as authoritative absolutes and would lead to noncollaborative tapers."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:cdc-2016] CDC 2022 explicitly states these recommendations "are not intended to be used as an inflexible, rigid standard of care."[ref:cdc-2022]

≥ 50 MME/day — the primary reassessment guidepost (not a pharmacologic inflection). Pause and carefully reassess benefits versus risks; implement additional precautions (increased follow-up frequency); and offer naloxone.[ref:cdc-2022] CDC 2022 uses the language "offer naloxone" rather than "mandate co-prescribing."[ref:cdc-2022]

Above 50 MME/day — risk continues to increase with dose. The 2022 guideline does not specify a single numeric upper threshold but emphasizes avoiding dosage increases unlikely to improve pain or function relative to increasing risk.[ref:cdc-2022] The older 2016 "avoid ≥ 90 MME without specialist involvement" framing was deliberately softened — specialist consultation is best practice for complex high-dose cases, not a CDC-mandated requirement at any specific number.[ref:cdc-2016][ref:cdc-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023]

State-specific thresholds Some states have their own numeric mandates (Washington requires pain-specialist consultation before exceeding 120 MME/day, for example) — this is state regulation, not CDC guidance.[ref:cdc-2022] Check your state's specific rules with your compliance office.

Document clinical rationale for any dose above the 50 MME guidepost — the documentation, not the number, is what protects you and the patient.[ref:cdc-2022]

items.question: The patient is on 120 MME/day and has been stable for years. Do I taper them?
items.answer_html:
Stability on a long-standing dose is meaningful clinical data, not a license for indefinite passive prescribing. Do not taper at the first visit.[ref:cdc-2022]

The harms of abrupt taper are well-quantified. Agnoli (JAMA 2021, n=113,618) found that opioid dose tapering of patients on stable, long-term, higher-dose therapy was associated with adjusted IRR 1.68 for overdose, 2.28 for mental-health crisis, and 3.30 for suicide attempt; absolute risk increases were largest at the highest baseline doses (≥300 MME/day).[ref:agnoli-jama-2021] CDC 2022 Recommendation 5: "opioid therapy should not be discontinued abruptly"; FDA has issued a prescriber warning about hazards of rapid dose reduction including withdrawal, psychological distress, and suicidality.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:fda-oxycodone]

Counterpoint nuance The evidence is strongest for rapid taper and discontinuation. CDC 2022 notes that when patients agree to taper and it is done gradually (≤ 10% per month) with behavioral support, outcomes including pain, function, and quality of life can actually improve.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:agnoli-jama-2021][ref:lin-nejm-2025] For patients on opioids ≥ 1 year, tapers can take months to years.[ref:arnold-aafp-2023] Avoid the equal-and-opposite error of locking in indefinite continuation.

At the first visit: complete the intake assessment, establish the relationship, prescribe with full documentation of your awareness of the dose and your clinical rationale for continuation, and use the e-consult to get pain management eyes on the chart. A reasonable consult ask: "Patient stable on X MME/day for Y years. PDMP and UDS reviewed; functional status [description]; concurrent benzodiazepines [yes/no]. Please review current regimen and advise on appropriateness, whether a structured gradual taper is indicated, and whether ongoing co-management is appropriate."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:coffin-am-2022]

items.question: Should I offer naloxone?
items.answer_html:
Yes — CDC 2022 uses the language offer naloxone rather than mandate co-prescribing ("offer" can mean prescribing or directly providing it).[ref:cdc-2022] The CDC 2022 list of indications:[ref:cdc-2022]

≥ 50 MME/day

Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription CDC specifies benzodiazepines, not "any CNS depressant" — the broader CNS-depressant principle is clinically sound but slightly broader than the guideline indication.[ref:cdc-2022]

History of substance use disorder or prior overdose

Sleep-disordered breathing Listed as a separate CDC 2022 risk factor.[ref:cdc-2022]

Risk of returning to a high dose to which the patient has lost tolerance Post-incarceration release, during or after tapering — a CDC 2022 indication that is often missed.[ref:cdc-2022]

Household members at risk of accidental exposure Maps to CDC's recommendation to provide overdose-prevention education to household members; the patient-level naloxone indication and the household-education recommendation overlap but are not identical.[ref:cdc-2022]

Document that you offered or prescribed naloxone, that you counseled on administration, and that the household has access. This is standard-of-care language consistent with CDC 2022, not a specific institutional mandate.[ref:cdc-2022]

faqs.title: Inheriting a high-dose patient — continuity, documentation, and the e-consult

items.question: Can I continue prescribing at this dose while I arrange the e-consult?
items.answer_html:
Yes — do not abruptly discontinue or reduce at the first visit while awaiting specialist input. Continuity of an established regimen while arranging appropriate oversight is clinically and ethically defensible, and is the position of CDC 2022 Recommendation 5.[ref:cdc-2022] The CDC further warns payers and health systems should not "penalize clinicians for accepting new patients who are receiving opioids for chronic pain," and the FDA has issued a prescriber warning about the hazards of rapid taper or sudden discontinuation in physically dependent patients (acute withdrawal, pain exacerbation, serious psychological distress, and suicidal ideation).[ref:cdc-2022][ref:fda-oxycodone]

Conditional on absence of life-threatening signals Continuity is defensible only when there are no acute safety signals at the visit — sedation, respiratory depression, slurred speech, evidence of active diversion. If those are present, dose reduction or discontinuation may be warranted even at the first encounter.[ref:cdc-2022]

Continuity is a bridge, not an endpoint The CDC expects the new clinician to establish treatment goals (including functional goals) and reassess within 1–3 months. Continuity gets you safely past the first visit; the structured benefit-risk reassessment is still the work.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:coffin-am-2022]

Document the full first-visit framework — not just the four-item intake checklist. The CDC 2022 + Coffin 2022 + VA/DoD 2022 synthesis expects:[ref:cdc-2022][ref:coffin-am-2022][ref:sandbrink-aim-2023][ref:sonoda-aafp-2025] (1) continued regimen absent life-threatening signals; (2) MME calculation and documentation; (3) PDMP review (mandatory under NY I-STOP, initial-plus-quarterly under NJ PMP);[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1] (4) baseline UDS (non-punitive); (5) offer naloxone; (6) screen for OUD (TAPS, DAST) and mental-health comorbidities;[ref:cdc-2022] (7) functional-status assessment (PEG scale) and treatment goals;[ref:cdc-2022] (8) concurrent-benzodiazepine check; (9) document rationale for continuation and the plan for reassessment;[ref:coffin-am-2022] (10) arrange pain-management consultation if function is not improving, documentation is limited, or dosage is well above 50 MME without clear justification;[ref:cdc-2016][ref:cdc-2022] (11) follow-up within 1–3 months.[ref:cdc-2022]

items.question: What is the e-consult ask at high dose?
items.answer_html:
The structured ask below is institutional best practice consistent with the CDC 2022 assessment domains; no specific guideline (CDC, AAFP, ASAM, VA/DoD) prescribes a fixed e-consult template. Treat it as a workflow scaffold, not a guideline-mandated form.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:cdc-2016][ref:coffin-am-2022]

Be specific: "Patient inherited on [X] MME/day of [agent] for [indication]. Prior pain management documentation: [present / limited / absent]. PDMP: [findings]. UDS: [confirms prescribed agent / unexpected finding]. Functional status: [PEG scores; brief description of work, ADLs, pain interference]. Concurrent benzodiazepine: [yes / no, plus dose / indication if yes]. Treatment goals discussed and documented. Please review current regimen and advise: (1) whether the dose is appropriate for the indication, (2) whether a structured gradual taper is indicated and at what rate, and (3) whether ongoing co-management is appropriate."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:coffin-am-2022]

Where the picture suggests OUD rather than (or alongside) chronic pain, reframe the consult: "Patient with chronic pain and possible OUD — please advise on MOUD candidacy and transition plan," and route to addiction medicine rather than pain management.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:harris-jama-2026]

items.question: The patient tells me their prior doctor "always" prescribed this and they'll go elsewhere if I change anything.
items.answer_html:
Acknowledge the anxiety without making promises you can't keep: "I understand this medication has been important to your quality of life and I'm not here to take anything away from you today. I do need to complete my own assessment as your new provider, and I want to make sure we're doing this in a way that protects you."[ref:arnold-aafp-2023][ref:sandbrink-aim-2023]

Do not let the threat of patient departure drive clinical decisions, but do not treat the threat as noise either — patient distress at the prospect of dose changes is a clinically meaningful signal. It may reflect undertreated pain, anxiety, or features of opioid use disorder, all of which warrant assessment rather than dismissal.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:sandbrink-aim-2023][ref:blanco-lancet-2019] Document not just the threat but the clinical assessment of what is driving it.

The AAFP summary of CDC 2022 captures the principle: "physicians should acknowledge the discordance, express empathy, and implement patient-centered treatment changes without abandoning the patient."[ref:arnold-aafp-2023] CDC 2022 explicitly warns against dismissing patients on the basis of opioid-related concerns and states clinicians have a "responsibility to provide or arrange for coordinated management."[ref:cdc-2022]

faqs.title: Concurrent opiates and benzodiazepines — high-risk, but not automatic discontinuation

items.question: How dangerous is this combination?
items.answer_html:
The combination carries elevated overdose risk, but the magnitude is range-bound and time-dependent. Across the literature, concurrent opioid-benzodiazepine prescribing is associated with roughly a 2–5× increase in overdose-related outcomes depending on population, outcome measured, dose, and duration.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:sun-bmj-2017][ref:cho-jgim-2020][ref:hernandez-jamaopen-2018] The CDC 2022 case-cohort citation is at the high end ("near-quadrupling of risk for overdose death"); a privately insured cohort (Sun BMJ 2017) found OR 2.14 for opioid overdose-related ED visit/hospitalization; a Kaiser cohort (Cho JGIM 2020) found only ~20% increase.[ref:sun-bmj-2017][ref:cho-jgim-2020]

Time-dependence is the operationally important nuance A Medicare Part D analysis (Hernandez JAMA Open 2018) found HR 5.05 in the first 90 days of concurrent use, dropping to non-significant after 180 days of stable concurrent use.[ref:hernandez-jamaopen-2018] Long-term, stable, low-dose concurrent regimens carry meaningfully lower (still elevated) risk than newly-started concurrent regimens — which is exactly why "destabilize the inherited stable patient" is the wrong move.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:hernandez-jamaopen-2018]

Mechanism is more nuanced than "synergistic" Benzodiazepines at standard doses have minimal effects on ventilation alone; they primarily contribute to overdose risk via sedation, loss of airway protective reflexes, and upper airway obstruction rather than classic pharmacodynamic synergy on central respiratory drive.[ref:gershuny-bja-2025][ref:florian-jama-2022] A 2025 FDA-sponsored RCT in healthy volunteers found that midazolam + oxycodone did not significantly decrease hypercapnic ventilatory response compared with oxycodone alone, but did increase resting end-tidal CO₂ and caused 60% of participants to fall asleep or snore (vs 0% on oxycodone alone).[ref:gershuny-bja-2025] Operational language: benzodiazepines potentiate opioid-induced respiratory depression through complementary mechanisms.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:horsfall-bcpt-2017]

The FDA issued class-wide boxed warnings on the combination in 2016 (all opioid analgesics, opioid cough products, and all benzodiazepines), warning that concomitant use "may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death."[ref:fda-oxycodone][ref:fda-triazolam][ref:fda-lorazepam][ref:hadland-peds-2024] One important nuance from a 2017 FDA clarification: patients with OUD who need buprenorphine or methadone should still receive these medications even if already on benzodiazepines, because withholding MOUD carries greater risk.[ref:hadland-peds-2024]

The CDC 2022 guideline (Recommendation 11) is Category B ("particular caution"), not Category A ("avoid") — softened from the 2016 framing — and explicitly states that "in specific situations benzodiazepines can be beneficial, and that stopping benzodiazepines can be destabilizing" and that "long-term, stable use might be safer than erratic, unpredictable use."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:cdc-2016]

items.question: The patient has legitimate indications for both. What do I do?
items.answer_html:
The first-visit pattern is bridge both, document, refer — not "choose one." No major guideline (CDC 2022, VA/DoD 2022, ASAM 2025) recommends withholding one of two chronically prescribed medications at the first visit when the patient has legitimate indications for both and is on a stable regimen.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo] Withholding the benzodiazepine risks withdrawal seizure; withholding the opioid risks withdrawal and uncontrolled pain. CDC 2022 explicitly warns against abrupt changes that destabilize patients; VA/DoD 2022 cautions against abrupt benzodiazepine discontinuation due to seizure and death risk.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022]

At the first visit:

(1) Continue both medications at current doses if the patient is on a long-term stable regimen.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022]

(2) Document the combination as a known risk and the risk-benefit assessment — dose, duration, indication, prior taper attempts, functional status, prior overdose, household risk, pain control, anxiety control.[ref:cdc-2022]

(3) Prescribe naloxone ASAM 2025 makes naloxone provision a strong recommendation for all patients co-prescribed opioids and benzodiazepines.[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:brunner-jgim-2025]

(4) Check the PDMP per state (NY: every prescription; NJ: initial plus quarterly).[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1]

(5) Plan a shorter-interval follow-up (2–4 weeks rather than 3 months) given the higher-risk regimen.[ref:cdc-2022]

(6) Initiate (not necessarily complete) specialist consultation if there is concern about the indication for either medication or if tapering is being considered. Specialist input — psychiatry for the benzodiazepine or pain management for the opioid — is strongly recommended, not mandated by any major guideline. The PCP may continue managing both prescriptions with appropriate documentation, naloxone, PDMP monitoring, and reassessment.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:brunner-jgim-2025]

Reassessment cadence ASAM 2025 recommends risk-benefit reassessment at least every 3 months for any patient on chronic concurrent opioid + benzodiazepine therapy, regardless of stability.[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:brunner-jgim-2025]

If OUD is present alongside the combination ASAM 2025 explicitly recommends stabilizing on MOUD (buprenorphine or methadone) before initiating a benzodiazepine taper. The OUD pathway takes priority over benzo deprescribing in this subset.[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:brunner-jgim-2025][ref:cdc-2022]

Refusing both at the first visit risks destabilizing the patient and is explicitly cautioned against by the CDC 2022 OWG.[ref:cdc-2022]

items.question: Can I just taper the benzo?
items.answer_html:
Not unilaterally at the first visit. CDC 2022 states that abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause "rebound anxiety, hallucinations, seizures, delirium tremens, and, rarely, death"; ASAM 2025 instructs that clinicians "should not discontinue BZDs abruptly in patients who are likely to be physically dependent."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:brunner-jgim-2025] The NEJM review on benzodiazepine dependence recommends gradual discontinuation over 4–8 weeks minimum, with hospitalization considered for very high doses (≥ 100 mg diazepam-equivalent daily).[ref:soyka-nejm-2017]

The reason not to start a taper at the first visit is more than seizure risk — the first visit lacks the therapeutic relationship, baseline assessment, and coordination needed for safe tapering. Successful deprescribing requires patient education, shared decision-making, and frequent dialogue.[ref:aafp-robertson-2023]

Sequencing — keep the tapers separate Soyka NEJM is explicit: "concurrent opioid detoxification is not recommended" during benzodiazepine tapering; the opioid dose should be kept stable through the benzodiazepine reduction period.[ref:soyka-nejm-2017]

That said, the CDC 2022 guideline shifted from the 2016 framing (which suggested it "might be safer and more practical to taper opioids first") to a more individualized 2022 approach.[ref:cdc-2016][ref:cdc-2022] A 2023 scoping review of 26 guidelines found zero provided specific guidance on deprescribing sequence, and the four that addressed it gave conflicting recommendations.[ref:wang-jcm-2023] Sequencing should be individualized.

Coordination with psychiatry is recommended but not mandated — CDC says "communicate with mental health professionals managing the patient." If no psychiatrist is involved, the PCP or an addiction-medicine specialist can manage the taper.[ref:cdc-2022]

faqs.title: UDS shows something unexpected — next steps

items.question: The UDS is positive for cocaine. Do I stop the opiate today?
items.answer_html:
Confirm with send-out testing before drawing a clinical conclusion. The reflex "do not prescribe at this visit" is not CDC-supported — CDC 2022 explicitly states that toxicology testing "should not be used in a punitive manner" and that "clinicians should not dismiss patients from care on the basis of a toxicology test result."[ref:cdc-2022] An observational analysis found that a stimulant-positive UDS in patients on long-term opioids was not significantly associated with subsequent opioid-related ED visits or overdose deaths within 90 days, but was associated with LTOT discontinuation — suggesting that reflex withholding may be more reflexive than evidence-based.[ref:appa-dad-2024]

Cocaine alone does not diagnose OUD Cocaine use indicates a stimulant use disorder, polysubstance use, or co-occurring substance use disorders may be present — apply a comprehensive SUD evaluation using DSM-5 criteria across substance classes, not OUD-only screening. MOUD is appropriate only if OUD criteria are met; the stimulant use disorder itself also requires its own management.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:hasin-ajp-2022][ref:dsm5-2022]

Operational sequence:

(1) Confirm the result with LC-MS/MS where it will change management. (2) Have a direct, non-punitive safety conversation: "I'm concerned about your safety if these substances are combined. Tell me what's been going on."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aapm-argoff-2018] (3) Conduct a structured SUD assessment (TAPS, DAST-10, NIDA Quick Screen) and apply DSM-5 criteria. (4) Prescribe naloxone and add fentanyl test strip education (the contemporary illicit-supply context is relevant even when fentanyl is not detected).[ref:cdc-2022] (5) Consider MOUD if OUD criteria are met; refer for stimulant use disorder treatment in parallel.[ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:wakeman-jamaopen-2020] (6) Conduct an individualized risk-benefit analysis on continuing the prescribed opioid; if continuing, document enhanced monitoring (shorter prescription intervals, more frequent UDS) and naloxone provision. (7) Do not reflexively discontinue.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:kennedy-plos-2022][ref:babu-nejm-2019]

The NEJM review captures the principle: "opioid use disorder in patients with chronic pain is an indication for more care rather than less," and a punitive approach "places patients at greater risk for overdose if they transition from pharmaceutical opioids to illicit ones."[ref:babu-nejm-2019][ref:kennedy-plos-2022] Use person-first language in documentation — "patient with substance use disorder," not "abuser" or "addict" — and avoid volitional-failure framing.[ref:volkow-jamapsych-2019][ref:gibson-asam-2024]

items.question: The UDS is positive for fentanyl but the patient is not prescribed it.
items.answer_html:
This is a high-acuity finding that warrants confirmation and a structured response, not a punitive one. CDC 2022 notes that "testing for fentanyl is not available in widely used toxicology assays, potentially leading to false assurance" — meaning when fentanyl is detected, it was likely tested for specifically, which increases the reliability of the result.[ref:cdc-2022] Confirm with LC-MS/MS where the result will change management.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:stolbach-jmt-2022]

Drug-supply cross-contamination caveat Fentanyl is increasingly present in counterfeit pills and mixed into non-opioid drugs (cocaine, methamphetamine, benzodiazepines); the patient may not have knowingly used an opioid. This does not reduce the acuity of the finding, but it changes the counseling approach — the safety conversation is "the supply is contaminated and you may have been exposed without knowing," not just "you used street opioids."[ref:cdc-2022]

The four-element response, framed as a safety intervention rather than a punitive one:

(1) Naloxone prescribe and counsel on use; ensure household access.[ref:cdc-2022] (2) Fentanyl test strip education the harm-reduction intervention recommended in CDC 2022 framing of unexpected fentanyl findings.[ref:cdc-2022] (3) Structured OUD assessment apply DSM-5 11 criteria with pain-adjusted approach (see the OUD FAQ).[ref:hasin-ajp-2022][ref:cdc-2022] (4) MOUD discussion framed as safety intervention; route to addiction medicine.[ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:cdc-2022]

Abrupt discontinuation of the prescribed opioid in this scenario carries the highest overdose risk — Kennedy 2022 found AHR 3.18 (95% CI 1.87–5.40) for overdose among patients with OUD discontinued from prescribed opioids without OAT.[ref:kennedy-plos-2022] Continuity with close monitoring and an active referral in process is safer than termination from the practice.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:babu-nejm-2019][ref:fda-oxycodone] Engage with empathy and use person-first language.[ref:volkow-jamapsych-2019][ref:gibson-asam-2024]

faqs.title: Concerning PDMP patterns — how to respond

items.question: I see fills from three different pharmacies. Is that diversion?
items.answer_html:
It is a pattern that warrants clarification, not a confirmed finding. CDC 2022 flags multiple pharmacies as part of concerning patterns but does not define a specific numeric threshold; research has used ≥ 4 pharmacies in 90 days as a risk-behavior threshold.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:greene-ajadd-2017] Three is a reasonable clinical heuristic but should not be presented as a validated threshold.

Common legitimate explanations include pharmacy closures, mail-order vs retail splits, travel, formulary or network changes, and specialty pharmacy requirements.[ref:cdc-2022] Ask directly and document the answer. A pattern of cash-pay fills at multiple locations without a coherent explanation is more concerning, but cash-pay alone is not the same as diversion (PDMPs capture cash-pay fills regardless of insurance status).[ref:cdc-2022][ref:manasco-pds-2016]

Where the pattern is unexplained, confirm with send-out UDS to establish whether the patient is actually taking the prescribed medication. If the pattern remains unexplained and confirmed by UDS, this is a case for e-consult before continuing — but the pathway is investigation and care coordination, not dismissal.[ref:cdc-2022]

items.question: What do I document when I find a PDMP concern?
items.answer_html:
Document exactly what you found (dates, prescribers, pharmacies, quantities), what you asked the patient, what they told you, and your clinical assessment. This documentation protects both the patient and the clinician regardless of what you decide.[ref:cdc-2022]

The CDC 2022 framing for PDMP concerns: PDMP information should be used in the context of other clinical information (history, physical findings, relevant testing) rather than as a standalone determinant; PDMP-generated risk scores have not been validated against clinical outcomes; and "clinicians should not dismiss patients from their practice on the basis of PDMP information."[ref:cdc-2022][ref:perry-add-2022]

If you choose to continue prescribing despite a flag, document your reasoning, the patient's explanation, the steps taken to coordinate with other prescribers, and any monitoring intensifications (shorter intervals, additional UDS, naloxone). If you choose not to prescribe, document the alternatives offered (non-opioid pain management, pain-specialist referral, bridge prescription with short-interval follow-up) and the safety plan for the patient — refusing to prescribe is defensible, but refusing to provide any care pathway is not.[ref:cdc-2022]

faqs.title: Early refills, lost medications, escalating contact

items.question: How many early refill requests trigger a formal response?
items.answer_html:
Provenance note The escalation framework below is a practice-level convention; no published guideline (CDC 2022, VA/DoD 2022, APS/AAPM, ASAM) specifies numeric early-refill thresholds. The closest published data point is APS/AAPM 2009: "one or two episodes of unauthorized opioid escalations" in low-risk patients can often be managed with education and enhanced monitoring, while "4+ previous aberrant drug-related behaviors" (any type, not just early refills) is the inflection point for substance-use-disorder concern.[ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009][ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023] CDC 2022 deliberately avoids rigid thresholds and emphasizes individualized clinical judgment.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023]

1 request — warrants a conversation and documentation. Kern PM 2020: ~10% of opioid patients have an early refill (≥ 15% early relative to days' supply); 75% of those patients have only one. A single early refill is common and often benign — vacation prep, dose adjustments, 14-day refills written as 30-day supply.[ref:kern-pm-2020][ref:liebschutz-jamaim-2017]

2+ in 12 months — practice-level convention triggering a formal documented conversation within the CS agreement framework, a UDS, and a PDMP review. Note: PDMP review is mandatory under NY I-STOP before every prescription (not just at this threshold), and required in NJ at initial-plus-quarterly cadence under NJSA 45:1-46.1; the 2+ trigger does not lower the regulatory baseline.[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1] UDS should also be part of baseline monitoring for all chronic-opiate patients, not triggered only by behavioral flags.[ref:cdc-2016][ref:cdc-2022][ref:jannetto-jalm-2018]

3+ in 12 months — practice-level convention warranting e-consult before continuation. Apply the differential below before assuming misuse.

Differential before interpretation Aberrant behaviors have a differential diagnosis — they may reflect undertreated pain, psychiatric comorbidity, social stressors, or opioid use disorder, not exclusively misuse.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009] Document the pattern; interpret only after clinical assessment. CDC 2022 specifically warns against using monitoring findings in a punitive manner.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023]

Document each instance at the time it occurs — date of request, reason given, clinical response, monitoring actions taken. Patterns are only visible in retrospect if the individual events are in the chart.[ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009][ref:webster-pmr-2015][ref:acoem-2017-otc]

items.question: The patient calls repeatedly between visits asking for early refills, dose increases, or exceptions. How do I manage this?
items.answer_html:
Frequent between-visit contact around controlled substances is a behavioral signal warranting documentation and clinical assessment — not an automatic indicator of misuse. Aberrant behaviors are well-established in the pain-management literature (Merlin 2018 Delphi: "asking for an increase in opioid dose" and "using more opioid medication than prescribed" are among the most common concerning behaviors in long-term opioid therapy), but the differential still includes inadequate pain control, anxiety, functional decline, and psychosocial crisis alongside misuse and diversion.[ref:paice-jco-2016][ref:kaye-painphys-2017a][ref:kaye-painphys-2017b][ref:merlin-jgim-2018][ref:cdc-2022][ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009]

Establish a clear protocol and communicate it once, in writing: routine controlled-substance management decisions (refill timing, dose adjustments, formulary substitutions) are addressed at scheduled visits, not by phone or portal message. Urgent clinical concerns — acute pain crisis, withdrawal symptoms due to a pharmacy-supply issue, concerning new symptoms — will be triaged appropriately. Preserve the structure for routine management while keeping an exception pathway for genuinely urgent clinical situations; a blanket refusal to address any between-visit CS concerns can create safety risks (acute pain, withdrawal, missed deterioration).[ref:cdc-2022][ref:alford-jama-2013][ref:acoem-2017-otc][ref:bruce-cid-2017]

Document that this was communicated, and document the differential when interpreting the pattern. CDC 2022's framing: monitoring findings are signals to investigate, not verdicts to act on.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:arnold-aafp-2023]

items.question: The patient says their medication was stolen. What are my obligations?
items.answer_html:
Federal law (21 CFR §1306.04, §1306.11–12; 21 USC §829) does not categorically prohibit a practitioner from issuing a new prescription when a patient reports a lost or stolen Schedule II medication. The validity of any new prescription is governed by §1306.04 — it must be issued for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice.[ref:cfr-1306-04][ref:cfr-1306-11][ref:cfr-1306-12][ref:usc-21-829][ref:neuman-anesth-2020][ref:osborne-jmwh-2017]

Most institutions and practices nonetheless adopt a no-replacement policy for lost or stolen Schedule II medications as a risk-management standard.[ref:asam-risk2024][ref:acoem-2017-otc][ref:webster-pmr-2015] That is institutional policy, not federal regulation; communicate it honestly. Suggested phrasing: "Our practice doesn't replace lost or stolen Schedule II prescriptions as a matter of policy. The DEA framework allows me clinical discretion, but our institutional standard is no replacement, and that's how I have to handle this."[ref:asam-risk2024][ref:acoem-2017-otc]

The ACOEM Opioid Treatment Contract template includes the language: "I agree to immediately report stolen opioid medication(s) to the police. My provider will also produce a police report if requested to do so."[ref:acoem-2017-otc] Offering to file a police report with the patient creates an external record and is occasionally relevant; document the offer and the patient's response regardless of whether a report is filed. The police report is a documentation step, not a replacement trigger.[ref:acoem-2017-otc]

A single loss event is not disqualifying for future prescribing — APS/AAPM 2009 supports managing isolated aberrant episodes with education and enhanced monitoring rather than discontinuation.[ref:aps-aapm-chou-2009][ref:cdc-2022][ref:merlin-jgim-2018] A single-loss-event response: document the event, review the PDMP, consider UDS, have a secure-storage conversation, and note in the CS agreement file. Repeated lost-prescription reports — especially clustered with other risk markers — change the clinical picture and warrant escalation.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:merlin-jgim-2018]

Verify your institution's policy and current state requirements with your compliance office at the time of use; regulations are subject to legislative updates.

faqs.title: When chronic pain management becomes OUD — recognizing and responding

items.question: How do I distinguish chronic pain requiring opiates from OUD?
items.answer_html:
Chronic pain and OUD are not mutually exclusive — co-occurrence is common enough that it should always be assessed. The accurate framing, however, is that the majority of chronic-pain patients on long-term opioid therapy do not meet OUD criteria: studies using DSM-5 in LTOT cohorts find any-OUD prevalence of 21–27% and moderate-to-severe OUD at 4–9%.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:archambault-jcn-2024][ref:hasin-ajp-2022]

Use the formal DSM-5 11-criterion checklist rather than an informal sign list. The criteria for OUD include: taking opioids in larger amounts or longer than intended; persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down; excessive time spent obtaining/using/recovering; craving; failure to fulfill role obligations; continued use despite social or interpersonal problems; giving up activities; use in physically hazardous situations; continued use despite physical or psychological problems caused or exacerbated by opioids; tolerance; and withdrawal.[ref:dsm5-2022][ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022] Severity: 2–3 criteria = mild; 4–5 = moderate; ≥ 6 = severe.[ref:dsm5-2022]

Pain-adjusted application is critical DSM-5 specifies that tolerance and withdrawal do not count toward an OUD diagnosis if they occur solely in the context of opioids taken as prescribed. The challenge is exactly the diagnostic ambiguity that pain-adjusted instruments (Hasin AJP 2022) attempt to address — distinguish behaviors driven by therapeutic intent (taking medication to manage pain as prescribed) from nontherapeutic motives (compulsive use, loss of control).[ref:hasin-ajp-2022][ref:dsm5-2022][ref:vadod-2022]

Document which DSM-5 criteria are met and whether each behavior is driven by therapeutic intent versus nontherapeutic motives. Hallmarks specifically highlighted in the LTOT literature include emotional volatility, taking more medication than prescribed, using opioids for reasons other than pain, frequent loss of medication, and early refills — but apply the differential before concluding OUD.[ref:babu-nejm-2019][ref:cdc-2022]

items.question: If I think this is OUD, what is the pathway?
items.answer_html:
MOUD — medication for opioid use disorder — significantly outperforms taper or discontinuation for outcomes including overdose survival. The three MOUDs are not equivalent:[ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:wakeman-jamaopen-2020][ref:wakeman-nejmevid-2022][ref:lim-plosone-2022][ref:blanco-lancet-2019]

Buprenorphine all-cause mortality reduction RR 0.34 (95% CI 0.26–0.45, ~60% reduction); first-line for primary care because office-based induction is feasible.[ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:buresh-bmj-2021]

Methadone all-cause mortality reduction RR 0.47 (95% CI 0.41–0.54, ~50% reduction); highest retention in network meta-analysis.[ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:lim-plosone-2022] Federally restricted to SAMHSA-certified Opioid Treatment Programs for outpatient OUD treatment.[ref:calcaterra-jamaopen-2025]

Naltrexone Oral naltrexone is no more effective than placebo; extended-release injectable naltrexone shows benefit over no medication but is inferior to buprenorphine in intention-to-treat analyses due to the 7–10-day opioid-free induction barrier. Wakeman 2020 comparative effectiveness: only buprenorphine and methadone were associated with reduced overdose and opioid-related acute care vs no treatment; naltrexone, inpatient detox, and behavioral interventions showed no significant benefit at 3-month follow-up.[ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:wakeman-jamaopen-2020][ref:wakeman-nejmevid-2022]

Buprenorphine — primary care scope The X-waiver was eliminated in December 2022 by the Mainstreaming Addiction Treatment (MAT) Act; any practitioner with a standard DEA registration and Schedule III prescribing authority can now prescribe buprenorphine for OUD with no patient caps.[ref:lefevre-jabfm-2023][ref:acog-mate-2025][ref:varisco-japha-2023] The MATE Act requires 8 hours of training on substance use disorders for new or renewed DEA registrations (self-attestation).[ref:acog-mate-2025] State-level regulations may still impose additional requirements not aligned with the federal change — verify NY-specific and NJ-specific buprenorphine-prescribing requirements with your compliance office at the time of use.[ref:arnold-aafp-2023][ref:lefevre-jabfm-2023] Removing the X-waiver has increased the prescriber pool but has not yet translated into commensurate increases in patients receiving buprenorphine; interest, comfort, and systems-level barriers remain primary obstacles.[ref:christine-jamaopen-2024][ref:chua-nejm-2024][ref:ostrach-japha-2023]

Methadone — what PCPs can and cannot do A DEA-registered PCP cannot prescribe methadone for OUD to be filled at an outpatient pharmacy — outpatient methadone for OUD is restricted to SAMHSA-certified OTPs.[ref:calcaterra-jamaopen-2025][ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:cdc-2022] Important exceptions: (a) 72-hour rule — any clinician may administer (not prescribe) methadone for up to 72 hours to treat acute opioid withdrawal while arranging OTP referral; updated regulations allow a 3-day supply dispensed at one time;[ref:calcaterra-jamaopen-2025][ref:harris-jama-2026] (b) hospital exception — hospitalized patients can be initiated on or continued on methadone during inpatient stays;[ref:harris-jama-2026][ref:cdc-2022] (c) methadone for pain ≠ methadone for OUD — methadone CAN be prescribed by any DEA-registered clinician for a pain indication and filled at retail pharmacy, but not for OUD.[ref:calcaterra-jamaopen-2025] Active policy advocacy is exploring pharmacy-based methadone dispensing for OUD; not yet law.[ref:tschampl-jamaopen-2026]

The e-consult framing shifts: instead of "please review pain management plan," it becomes "patient with chronic pain and possible OUD — please advise on MOUD candidacy and transition plan," and routes to addiction medicine rather than pain management.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:harris-jama-2026]

Person-first language and NIDA terminology CDC 2022: "opioid use disorder is a chronic, treatable disease from which persons can recover"; ASAM and AAFP both emphasize compassionate, non-judgmental, person-first communication. Use "patient with opioid use disorder," not "opioid abuser" or "addict"; avoid volitional-failure language ("refuses to comply," "non-compliant"); reference NIDA's terminology guide for documentation standards.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:gibson-asam-2024][ref:kowalchuk-aafp-2024][ref:blanco-lancet-2019][ref:volkow-jamapsych-2019]

items.question: Can I continue the opiate while initiating an OUD evaluation?
items.answer_html:
Yes — do not abruptly discontinue while the evaluation is pending. This is one of the best-evidenced principles in the module. Kennedy PLoS Med 2022 (BC retrospective cohort): discontinuation of prescribed opioids was associated with increased overdose risk across all groups, with the highest risk among patients with OUD not receiving opioid agonist therapy (AHR 3.18, 95% CI 1.87–5.40).[ref:kennedy-plos-2022] Agnoli JAMA 2021: tapering of patients on stable LTOT was associated with adjusted IRR 1.68 for overdose and 2.28 for mental-health crisis.[ref:agnoli-jama-2021] CDC 2022 Recommendation 5: "opioid therapy should not be discontinued abruptly"; "patients prescribed opioids but unable to access ongoing care might be at risk for abrupt opioid discontinuation."[ref:cdc-2022] FDA prescriber warning on hazards of rapid dose reduction.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:fda-oxycodone] The fentanyl-contaminated illicit supply adds a layer of lethality not present in earlier eras.

Continuity with close monitoring and an active referral in process is safer than discontinuation without a plan.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:kennedy-plos-2022][ref:agnoli-jama-2021] Close monitoring should include PDMP checks per state, urine drug screening as clinically appropriate, shorter prescription intervals, and naloxone co-prescribing.[ref:cdc-2022]

Document the rationale: "Continuing current opioid regimen at [dose] with [interval] monitoring to prevent abrupt-discontinuation harms while OUD evaluation is completed and MOUD transition is arranged, per CDC 2022 Guideline Recommendation 5."[ref:cdc-2022] This is a bridging strategy, not indefinite continuation.

If concurrent benzodiazepine present alongside OUD ASAM 2025 recommends stabilizing on MOUD before initiating a benzodiazepine taper in OUD patients on a co-prescribed regimen — sequencing matters.[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:brunner-jgim-2025][ref:cdc-2022]
